items.body: The year of blue continues: blue art, blue music, blue moods. Klara Lewis‘ Opening is an azure version of the hue, twisting and turning like permutations seen beneath varying degrees of light. The first single and opening track “Ta Min Hand” establishes the baseline from which the album will drift, like a small vessel upon the sea. Even the music includes waves. A sweet melody emerges, loops and abrades. In “City,” solo piano plays over the sounds of traffic and conversation, momentarily pausing as if to listen to the other acoustic sources. Suddenly a more aggressive set of sounds conquers the sonic field, a helicopter of rovers and gears. The piano reenters, insistent, then the conversation, posing questions about where the attention turns in an economy of sonic competition. The more orchestral “Vaknar” (“Waking”) attempts to soothe, but the ground has already proven unstable. The looping continues, but the volume increases. Opening revels in juxtaposition and incremental shift. “Feel” and “Drip” were composed for Mika Taanila’s expressive film “Failed Emptiness,” which toys with expectations of light. As the album’s most abrasive piece, “Feel” stands in contrast to the melodies that haunt the earlier selections. The brief “Drip” is its polar opposite, nearly a dance piece, restricted only by its length, the connecting tissue a feedback drone emerging toward the end. “Tide,” by far the album’s longest piece at 11:37, is dedicated to Christine Ödlund’s painting “Dissolving Strawberry,” and is also on a compilation EP that finds connections between pigment and tone. While listening, one gleans melodies through gauze, origins obscured like fragments of forgotten lyrics. By “How Far?” abstraction begins to win over form, Lewis’ voice suddenly emerging in the center as another instrument. Furthering the sense of inversion, the set closer is called “Opening,” making one wonder if the title may mean an opening, such as a pathway or door; or the sense of opening one’s self to unpredictability or the divine. By the time the album ends, one has been led down multiple pathways, and even the trail of string has become tangled. To find one’s bearings, one must return to the beginning or plunge further into the unknown. (Richard Allen)

I put this album on every so often specifically because these tracks are the ones that I want to hear. I'm an ordinary fan who loves this compilation and I'm giving it five stars because that is what this music deserves.

items.body: Review by omphaloskepsis — When I picture the Mount Rushmore of Chamber Prog, I clearly see the colossal Universe Zero and Present rising above a foggy valley, carved into the mountain side. The thick mist of time obscures the other etched visages jutting from the far-side of the Mountain. The Fool Leading The Blind amazes me and I wonder..."Will Asceta approach Univers Zero and Present's greatness? Time will tell. Asceta's album The Fool Leading the Blind is a resplendent, melodic, and focused masterpiece of modern chamber rock and Rock in Opposition (RIO). The epic tapestry, fashioned by multi-instrumentalist and composer Rodrigo Maccioni, the Chilean ensemble crafts an intricate sound shroud knit together with awesome, seamless transitions. Bassoon, clarinets, viola, and English horn merge with a jazzy electric guitars, bass, and drums. Asceta's music doesn't percolate with as many dissonate passages as Univers Zero or Present. Don't get me wrong, Asceta sails through its share of breathtaking dissonate rapids. However, Asceta's The Fool Leading The Blind seems more focused on melodic movements...much like classical compositions from a couple centuries ago.The Title Suite: The opening 21-minute epic flows fluidly from eerie, atmospheric sound spheres to exhilarating crescendos. The dynamic Interplay of tracks like Temple of Mirrors and When They Arrive showcase tight counterpoints where no single instrument dominates, weaving impeccable sonic tapestries into complex patterns. Every track is a treat! Asceta's thought-provoking, sonic bouquet shimmers like shattered stain glass in a cathedral on fire. Highly recommended for lovers of Univers Zero and Present.

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — As soon as you start listening to Quickly Quickly Quickly, and their opening track, "Firebears", you are plunged into a sonic explosion you weren't prepared for; it is a surprise that stirs you in much the same way hearing classic 70s bands for the first time did. I was reminded of King Crimson, there is something epic about it, yet also dark and dangerous, and yet I also thought of Sonic Youth, who, incidentally, also feature two guitarists, a crucial element in creating that sonic canvas.The way the keyboards and guitars intertwine was also innovative, and that was nothing compared to what followed, as the McGowan brothers sing with such deep emotion and grit. This sets them apart from other bands that might be solid instrumentally but, at least to my ears, lack a distinctive signature. The arrangements constantly shift and adapt to the unfolding music, a progression that is hard to predict, with the vocals guiding the instruments as they collectively build the melody, reversing the usual dynamic.Contrasts emerge quickly; a more introspective section takes on a nearly jazzy feel, albeit indirectly, and the piano can be as laid-back as Neil Young during the moments when Crazy Horse was resting. Towards the end, at times I thought I heard the voice of Chris Cornell from Soundgarden, specifically during his band's psychedelic moments, and I found that same powerful vocal range, imbued with genuine emotion, once again in The Tea Club."The Eternal German Infant" presents a contrast between its instrumental power, a kind of restrained violence, and the vulnerability of the vocals; it then plunges into imagery woven from seemingly disjointed guitar, bass, and keyboard notes, with the guitar tearing at notes as if seeking a meeting point between the spirit of the voice and the music, a near-theatrical encounter."Mister Freeze" opens another door within the established framework, that dreamlike (or perhaps nightmarish) atmosphere, as if hundreds of crystal shards were parting to clear the way: an acoustic guitar paired with electric strumming that hangs like a curtain of stained glass catching the sunlight. The same notes repeat, yet with a certain decomposition, like fruit left too long in the summer sun. The subtlety of David Sylvian's solo work gains ground, casting a protective mantle, that sheltering sky spoken of by writer Paul Bowles, evoking a desert soundtrack: the organ, the strumming guitar... and one mask concealing another."I Shall Consume Everything" layers on intensity, steadily building tension; drums and a guitar join the keyboards, shifting from the style of the early Fripp (circa 1969) to the Greek echoes of Aphrodite's Child, until a guitar riff finally tears down what was built, driven by distortion, overlapping and repeating vocals, and rhythmic breaks that shatter the melody, causing it to quickly fade away......was any disintegration worthy of the name ever slow?

There are moments of great freedom, reminiscent of jazz scat singing, that shift into free-jazz passages blended with hard rock. This fusion, combined with the vocalist's delivery (which at times resembles a mystical, inverted prayer), reaches a new level of decibel intensity and opens up a new dimension for the saxophone within progressive heavy rock, distinct from the styles of Van der Graaf Generator (a feat that once seemed impossible) or Gong, two major touchstones for the instrument in this genre. Here, the fusion is more contemporary, yet Kalimba still retains melody and harmony, in abundance, while incorporating folk influences drawn from indigenous music.The instrumental sections still sound as improvised and fresh as when they must have been composed; when the band kicks into highly intricate, distorted rock, backed by the string section, the music gains added weight without losing any power; quite the opposite. Mart�n Pe�a holds his own as a vocalist, knowing exactly how to function as yet another instrument.Tiempos paralelos can serve as a summary of Cherc�n's musical approach, as the first part involves the saxophone and a sense of restraint, while the second features an uprising led by the guitar and a defiant vocal performance, delivering a solo reminiscent of Annie Haslam channeling Ian Gillan. "Las Mentiras del Muro" opens with a powerful foundation of drums and bass that reminded me of the overflowing energy of Rage Against the Machine, though the comparison stops at the vocals, as Mart�n Pe�a handles both the metal and progressive sections with the same care and precision found in the saxophone notes; the sax, for all its delicacy, sounds no less powerful and truly stands out as a key protagonist of the album."Relato de una obsesi�n", specifically its first part, titled "Quimera", features Eastern percussion and rhythms; the quintet achieves such a profound communion that they seem to act as one, wholly absorbed in the task of capturing their vision for posterity. The second part, "El orate," erupts, unleashing the inevitable, a tidal surge that can no longer be contained. It embodies that Eastern-inspired tensi�n, held taut to the point of infinity, until it finally meets the resistance it had ultimately sought, and that fiery blaze, which was in fact its very reason for being, is consumed.As if the ashes still held light and heat after the fire, the album's final track, "Colores," embodies a mysticism that retains its clarity, refusing to be blinded by its own nature, and one that learns and evolves, promising a future that will harvest the seeds sown in this auspicious debut.

items.body: Review by kenethlevine — "Have one on Me" appeared 4 years after the landmark "Ys", with part of the delay relating to nodules on the singer's vocal cords in 2009 induced no doubt in part by her untrained and untamed pipes. Perhaps in reaction to her improved health and in an attempt not to repeat the same mistakes too quickly, this triple album of 3 LP length parts highlights more instrumental acumen, that is to say, it actually has breaks where she rests her voice, and some are the highlights of their respective tracks, indeed sometimes the only redeeming feature on the likes of "Good Intentions Paving Co". Joanna also sings in a more classically skilled manner without abandoning that whimsy entirely, even piling vocalise on the aforementioned and the title cut. These modifications coincide with and even steer the production into rock and jazz realms in preference to the chambered directives of the pre nodular Joanna. Merged with a handful of her best tunes- "'81", "Baby Birch", "On a Good Day", "In California", "Go Long" and "Kingfisher" - it's worth toasting (along with her health) if not wholeheartedly lionizing.

items.body: Mezzo-soprano Aigul Akhmetshina has sung her fair share of notable female characters—femmes fatales like Carmen (Carmen) and Dalila (Samson et Dalila), and others more innocent like Angelina (La Cenerentola) or Olga (Eugene Onegin). Her newest project with Antonio Pappano on piano, Mujer Fatal, is a multifaceted commentary on womanhood. Mujer Fatal Amazon Presto Apple The program ranges well beyond the operatic repertoire, and the mix proves attractive. It opens with the title track, written specifically for Akhmetshina by Elena Roussanova and recorded here for the first time. Both singer and pianist express the impassioned side of the femme fatale, but Akhmetshina adds an unmistakable fearlessness as well. In the song’s middle section she gives us glimpses of its opposite: vulnerability. The two featured songs from Montsalvatge’s Canciones negras speak to Akhmetshina’s technique: nothing overtly flashy, but a clarity of pitch and diction that carries No. 1 (track 2). Her breath control in No. 4 (track 3) yields long, luxurious legato lines. The songs are well-paired, setting yearning against dreaming. Bésame mucho (track 6) is the most recognizable of the non-classical offerings. Jonathan Palmer Lakeland’s arrangement of Consuelo Velázquez’s bolero affords the singer a spotlight that she maximizes: her phrases are lithe and organic, and even when the piano introduces a more structured rhythmic accompaniment, she upholds the sultry air that is central to the song. Ravel‘s Pièce en forme de Habanera (track 8) is one of the most impressive tracks for its expressive and technical range. As with many of his works, the difficulty is hidden in the finer details, and such is the case here: the melismatic passages are tightly controlled yet come off as spontaneous. Several moments of pointed interjection from the duo surprise not because they are out of place, but because they push past the expected emotional intensity. Given the minimalism of some of his best-known piano works, Erik Satie and his Je te veux (track 9) reveal a very different side, one that the duo portrays effectively. The music here is decidedly emotive, at times even rhapsodic. Through the drama, we can appreciate the persuasiveness of Akhmetshina’s sweeping vocal lines. Tchaikovsky‘s None but the Lonely Heart (track 11) possesses a similar earnestness and gives Pappano a chance to shine. Compared to some of the other songs, the keyboard has a greater presence here, and it is a pleasure to hear Pappano and Akhmetshina in a well-informed partnership: the lines intertwine at times, but one never feels in the way of the other. Rimsky-Korsakov’s The Nightingale and the Rose (track 12) carries a sense of mystery in its opening piano interlude; Akhmetshina’s first solo, unaccompanied, builds further tension and suspense. One of the most striking aspects of the song is the sheer vocal range required, and she shows complete comfort capturing the piercing high notes as she evokes the quiet enigma of the lower ones. Aigul Akhmetshina. Photo © Lera Nurgalieva. Of the American selections, those from Gershwin and Bernstein stand out. The Man I Love (track 14) juxtaposes Pappano’s jazzy yet pensive suavity with Akhmetshina’s sumptuous timbre. While her singing does come off a little heavy-handed at times, it does justice to the meaning of the text. Somewhere (track 16) sees Akhmetshina at her most sensitive in a comforting reading. A serious issue with the digital version of the album is that it does not come with a booklet, which, in a program like this, is paramount for song texts and translations. The physical CD appears to include them. This misstep aside, the performances are exquisite and make a convincing case for Akhmetshina and Pappano’s artistic versatility. If you enjoyed this album, also hear Aigul Akhmetshina: Aigul | Joyce DiDonato: Songplay | Elīna Garanča: Sol y Vida | Isabel Leonard & Sharon Isbin: Alma Española The form can be filled in the actual website url. items.body: This is French cellist Astrig Siranossian’s fifth release on the Alpha label, and her earlier albums cover a wide-ranging repertoire in which she appears both as a chamber musician and as a soloist. Here she is joined by the London Symphony Orchestra and François-Xavier Roth for Elgar’s Cello Concerto, with Britten’s Cello Sonata, Bruch’s Kol Nidrei and Elgar’s Salut d’amour completing the program. Cello Concerto Amazon Presto Apple There are some ninety readily available recordings of the Elgar Cello Concerto, so Siranossian is entering a crowded field. Every new release is measured against Jacqueline du Pré’s legendary performance with Barbirolli and the LSO (Warner Classics), and that status is well earned — I know of few other concerto recordings in which the solo part is played with such overwhelmingly personal, emotional expression. Barbirolli’s accompaniment is just as involving. But it is fascinating to hear Elgar’s own 1928 recording with Beatrice Harrison (the composer conducting the New Symphony Orchestra, Warner Classics), where his less heart-on-sleeve leadership has a different but potent emotional effect. Recent performances tend to fall into two contrasting interpretive camps. Some are gentler and more emotionally restrained, such as Paul Watkins/BBC Philharmonic/Davis (Chandos), Gautier Capuçon/LSO/Pappano (Erato), and Daniel Müller-Schott/Oslo Philharmonic/Previn (Orfeo). Others embrace a more extroverted emotional approach like du Pré’s that is nevertheless their own, such as Pieter Wispelwey/Netherlands Radio Philharmonic/van Steen (Channel Classics), Steven Isserlis/Philharmonia/Paavo Järvi (Hyperion), and Johannes Moser/Suisse Romande/Manze (Pentatone). Siranossian’s interpretation falls into the latter category. Her playing, caught up close by Alpha’s engineers, draws a dazzling range of colors from the 1756 Gennaro Gagliano cello. Siranossian’s interpretive ideal is signaled in the opening recitative: marked fortissimo and nobilmente, the initial attack is ferocious and emotionally raw, the nobilmente honored through color and weight rather than any stiff-upper-lip reticence. Her first statement of the main theme is silvery and lithe, while the later restatement is full-toned and impassioned. The second movement (Lento – Allegro molto) brings a delicate, playful lightening of mood, answered by an Adagio of greater intensity, the playing more inward and contemplative, the cello’s color at times blanched and exhausted. The final movement returns to a more unreserved, impassioned manner, surveying darker regions of the score that others leave unexplored. The LSO, which has played this score more times than anyone can count, strives to match Siranossian’s intensity, but is sometimes hampered by Roth’s more objective leadership. There is compensation in hearing the score laid out with such transparency, allowing us to appreciate the craft of Elgar’s writing. Astrig Siranossian. I last wrote about Britten‘s Cello Sonata in a review of Sheku Kanneh-Mason’s 2025 Decca recording. That reading, like this one from Siranossian and pianist Nathanaël Gouin, a regular duo partner, leans into the tough modernity of Britten’s writing. If the Kanneh-Mason siblings find more playfulness in the second-movement Scherzo, Siranossian and Gouin more thoroughly uncover the darker musings of the third-movement Elegia, albeit at a significantly faster tempo. The Marcia lacks the menace Johannes Moser finds (with pianist Paul Rivinius, Hänssler), but the closing Moto perpetuo has ferocious momentum and drive, without eclipsing the unique energy and bravado of Rostropovich’s account with the composer (Decca). Bruch‘s Kol Nidrei is built around two Jewish melodies. The composer described the first as “an age-old Hebrew song of atonement”; the second, in D major, draws on “O weep for those that wept on Babel’s stream,” a song he called moving and truly magnificent. The only performance of the work I own is János Starker’s with the LSO led by Doráti (Eloquence). It is quite lovely, both pained and calming. Siranossian’s slightly slower reading is more sweetly voiced and more openly poignant. Elgar’s Salut d’amour makes a perfect digestif. Alpha’s engineering is excellent, and it is particularly good to hear the LSO away from the acoustically challenged Barbican Hall; the concerto sessions took place at LSO St Luke’s. The liner notes consist of a January 2026 interview in which Siranossian spends more time on what connects her cello (once owned by John Barbirolli) with the repertoire on the album than on the music itself. Nevertheless, after hearing this recording I intend to hear Siranossian’s earlier albums — recommended. items.body: Sixteen years in, Mondträume have a different singer, a double album and, for the first time, confirmed live dates. “Mind Games” came out on Alfa Matrix on 26 June 2026 as a 24-track 2CD, the Spanish synthpop project’s third album and its first full-length with Nicky Schulschenk on vocals. In this interview Pikotto talks about how the collaborations on the record doubled as an audition process, why a previously unreleased Bruderschaft remix ended up on it, and what the current line-up actually is. On that last point he corrects the record: Mondträume is a duo of himself and Schulschenk, with Madil Hardis and Ivan Derbenev friends and collaborators rather than members. Mind Games (Deluxe Edition) by MONDTRÄUME Mondträume interview Bernard: Mondträume turns 16 this year, and the lineup has changed almost completely since 2010 – Damasius Venys left for Mental Exile in 2020, Ivan Derbenev and Madil Hardis joined in 2022, and Nicky Schulschenk has fronted the band since “Heart Machine” in 2023. What’s the one thing about writing a Mondträume song that has never changed through all of that, and what’s changed the most? Pikotto: First of all, I’d like to thank you for inviting me to take part in this interview. It’s quite amazing to think that 16 years have already passed!!!!!! Where has all that time gone? Looking back, I think the one thing that has never changed is the passion and excitement I still feel when I create music. The melodies continue to move between melancholy and happiness, and I still have the same desire to make music that can touch people, make them feel something, and ultimately allow them to enjoy the journey through each song. That is something I don’t think will ever change. In that sense, I don’t really feel that I have changed as an artist. I think the journey has simply taken a different direction. The road may have turned, but the essence remains the same: the way I approach composition, the emotions behind the melodies, and above all, the desire to keep creating. The biggest difference is that today, those songs have a new voice. Nicky has brought a new dimension and a new identity to the music, but the heart of what I want to express through my compositions is still very much the same. So perhaps the direction has changed, but the feeling that started this journey 16 years ago is still there. And as long as I continue to feel that excitement when I hear a melody come to life, I don’t see that changing anytime soon. Bernard: “Lovers, Sinners & Liars” took five years to finish because of health issues you were dealing with at the time. Did that experience change how you pace yourself as a songwriter, and did any of it shape how “Mind Games” came together? Pikotto: Not at all. In fact, if anything had changed, I would say it has changed for the better. It feels almost like being given a second chance – a chance to climb out of a dark place and start believing again that things can get better. When someone is struggling with their health or going through difficult circumstances in life, you can reach a point where you simply don’t feel like doing anything. Everything can suddenly seem as if it has come to an end. I think that is one of the biggest mistakes we make as human beings. Deep down, we know we should keep fighting and moving forward, but sometimes there is something inside us that blocks us and makes it incredibly difficult to take that next step. And unfortunately, no matter how much we want to fight it, it can be very hard to overcome. With “Mind Games”, I knew from the very beginning that it was going to be a difficult journey. We had a new singer, a new musical direction, and a lot of things that were unfamiliar to us. That made me want to give everything I had to this album. And looking at everything that has happened since its release – the reviews, the comments from listeners, and even the Spotify statistics, where we went from around 3,000 monthly listeners to more than 15,000 – I honestly feel that we have achieved something really special. We also spent several weeks at number two on the GEWC Top 15 as one of the best albums on the chart, which was an incredible feeling. When you put all of that together and see the response that “Mind Games” has been receiving, I can honestly say that I’m extremely proud of what we have accomplished. I truly believe we have done a great job, and I’m very satisfied with the result. And above all, I have to thank Nicky from the bottom of my heart for coming on board this journey, getting on this ship with me, and helping me make all of this possible. I honestly couldn’t be happier to have him alongside me for this new chapter of Mondträume. Bernard: “Mind Games” runs to 24 tracks across two CDs. Why a double album rather than a shorter, tighter release, and how did you decide what made the final cut versus what got held back? Pikotto: Well, this was something Seba from Alfa Matrix (I like to take this opportunity to send him a big hello from here) and I discussed At first, I had the idea of releasing the albums separately: the third Mondträume album with the new official vocalist, and a second album that would be more like a “Pikotto & Friends” project… or something along those lines. Just one of those crazy ideas that occasionally goes through my head, haha! But in the end, Seba and I decided to put everything together as a double CD, and honestly, I’m really happy with how it turned out. I think it was the right decision. In fact, I designed the entire visual side of the booklet myself 🙂 So it was a very personal project for me, not only musically but visually as well. As for what was left out, there are a couple of songs that never quite came together in my mind the way I wanted them to. And then there’s another one that, to be completely honest, I simply forgot to include! With so many things going through my head, I was bound to forget something at some point. I’m a disaster. And it’s actually a great remix by the […] Gerrit Thomas of the song “I Need You Now”. So I promise that it won’t be forgotten forever – I’m planning to release it on a future EP dedicated to that song. I guess sometimes even the songs that don’t make it onto the album end up having a second life of their own. Bernard: The album brings in guest vocalists from District 13, Neon Space Men, Color Theory, and Antilav. How did each of those collaborations happen, and did you write with a specific voice in mind before reaching out, or after? Pikotto: Well, I actually used these collaborations as a way of searching for a new singer. During that period, I was trying to figure out what direction to take and how I could find the right voice for Mondträume. One day, while talking to a great fan of ours, Alain (who is also a wonderful person) he suggested that I should try looking for a new vocalist through collaborations like these. In fact, he was the one who put me in contact with the singers involved. “Pictures of You” was born during that particular period of my life, while I was creating these songs and experimenting with different voices. But the moment I heard Nicky’s voice, the vocal melody, and the way his voice blended with the musical foundation I had created, I immediately fell in love with the combination. At that moment, I already knew exactly who I wanted to become the new official voice of Mondträume. I made the proposal to him, and, well… you all know how the story ended. 🙂 So, to answer the second part of the question, yes – all of the musical foundations were created before I contacted the singers. The collaborations came afterwards, as part of the process of finding the voice that would ultimately lead Mondträume into this new chapter. Bernard: The record also includes a previously unreleased Mondträume remix made for Bruderschaft. What’s the story behind that remix, and why put it on this album instead of releasing it on its own? Pikotto: This is quite a delicate subject for me, and the first thing I would like to do is send a huge hug to the great Rexx, wherever he may be. I hope that he has finally found peace and is happy. As many of you will know, he sadly passed away after battling that terrible disease, cancer. It was a devastating loss for the music scene, and my deepest thoughts and strength go to his family and loved ones. I actually made this remix quite a long time ago, when Rexx contacted me and asked if I would like to take part in the project. I didn’t hesitate for a second. Rexx and I were basically the only two people who had heard that remix for a very long time. He had nothing but praise for it, and his words really encouraged me and gave me a lot of motivation. Unfortunately, though, He never seemed to find the right moment to release it. When I finished the third album, I contacted Rexx and asked for his permission to include the remix on the album. He kindly gave me his blessing, and for me, that was a huge honour. Including it on the album means much more to me than simply adding another remix. It is my way of keeping his memory alive and making sure that, in some small way, Rexx will always have a place within our music and within the history of Mondträume. I will always be grateful to him for that. Bernard: Nicky joined as vocalist on “Heart Machine” in December 2023. Two years and a full album later, is he still primarily a vocalist, or is he shaping arrangements and lyrics now too? Pikotto: Nicky is mainly responsible for the vocals, and the lyrics come entirely from his own creativity and imagination. As I mentioned before, I’m extremely happy with him. I think he has an incredible voice, and it fits the synthpop style of Mondträume perfectly. That said, there have been a few occasions when he has said to me, “Hey, what if you did the melody like this at this particular point?” And sometimes those little suggestions can actually lead us somewhere really interesting. The truth is that working with him is both very easy and a lot of fun. We understand each other really well, and the creative process feels very natural between us. In a relatively short time, I think we’ve also developed a really strong friendship, which makes everything even more enjoyable. At the end of the day, when you can work with someone, create music together, have a laugh along the way, and genuinely enjoy the process, I think you’ve found something pretty special. Bernard: Madil Hardis, who joined Mondträume in 2022, put out a solo charity EP called “Noel” that same year. How involved is he in Mondträume day to day now, and does the rest of the current lineup – him and Ivan Derbenev – have room for outside projects like that? Pikotto: I have a very strong friendship with both of them. They are not official members of Mondträume. Mondträume is a duo consisting of Pikotto and Nicky. It’s true that we did try to work together as a group for a while, but I eventually realised that it wasn’t really the direction I wanted to take Mondträume in. That doesn’t change the fact that I have a great friendship with both of them, and I’m very grateful for everything we have created together. Madil has an absolutely spectacular voice, and I’m sure we will continue working together on future collaborations and features. Bernard: Side-Line called Mondträume one of the strongholds of “the 3rd electropop wave” a few years back, and ranked your debut among the best synthpop albums of the last four decades. Sixteen years in, does that kind of legacy talk change how you approach a new record, or do you try to ignore it? Pikotto: For me, that was a huge honour. Being mentioned among some of the great albums with my very first album… just imagine! It was something truly incredible and something I will always be grateful for. But honestly, it doesn’t influence me when I’m creating new music. Of course, whenever I’m asked about Mondträume, I’m very happy to mention those achievements, but they are not something I think about when I sit down to compose a new album. What I always try to do is make every new song something special for the people who listen to us and, above all, make them feel something. That is actually my biggest concern – not whether an album will be considered one of the best, but whether I will manage to create something that connects emotionally with the listener. That is what really matters to me. And, so far, I think I’m achieving it. If, in the future, another Mondträume album is once again considered one of the best albums, I will obviously be incredibly grateful and very happy about it, and I certainly hope it happens. But, as I said, it’s not something I’m constantly looking out for or worrying about. I simply want to keep making music that makes people feel something. Everything else is a wonderful bonus. Bernard: You’ve kept an unmistakable 80s touch since day one. With 24 new tracks on “Mind Games,” was there ever a temptation to push further away from that reference point, or does the project only really work within it? Pikotto: I really love the music of the 80s, and I think that definitely comes through in my compositions. But it’s not really a question of whether I want to move away from that sound or not. When I sit down to compose, I simply let my hands and my mind do what they naturally want to do. The melodies that come to me often have that unmistakable 80s feeling, and I feel very comfortable working that way. It’s simply part of who I am as a composer and the musical language I’ve developed over the years. Maybe at some point the musical direction will change a little, who knows? But somehow, whenever I try to move too far away from it, my mind seems to travel straight back to the 80s because that’s where it feels most at home. Hahaha! I guess you can take the composer out of the 80s, but you can’t take the 80s out of the composer! Bernard: “Poisoned Love” was included on Side-Line’s “United 2 – The Odin Files” compilation for Ukraine this July. What made you say yes to that specific compilation, and would Mondträume take part in benefit releases like it again? Pikotto: I believe that compilations like these, created to support a meaningful cause (whether it’s helping those affected by war, fighting diseases, or raising awareness for important issues) are always worth supporting. Being able to contribute, even in a small way, is something I feel is very important. We all have the opportunity to make a difference, no matter how big or small our contribution may be, and I think we should all do our part whenever we can. Music has always had the power to bring people together, inspire solidarity, and support those who need it most. If a song, an album, or a compilation can help achieve that, then I’m more than happy to be involved. And that also answers your second question: yes, absolutely. I will continue to participate in these kinds of projects whenever I have the opportunity. Supporting a good cause through music is something I will always be proud to do. Bernard: What’s next for Mondträume after “Mind Games” – live shows, a new lineup configuration, or time off before the next release? Pikotto: I hope the future has great things in store for us. As I mentioned earlier, the official Mondträume line-up is the one featured on this album: Nicky will be the voice at the front, while I will continue to focus on the music and production side. One of our main goals for 2027 is to start bringing Mondträume to the stage. In fact, we already have two shows confirmed: February 27th in Leeds (UK) and March 6th in Madrid. We are also very close to finalising another show in Mexico, and hopefully many more opportunities will follow. I’m also pleased to announce that we have recently signed a non-exclusive agreement with Dark Entries Spain, and our management will be handled by Barbara Banu. If anyone is interested in booking Mondträume, they are welcome to contact Barbara through her social media channels, or they can reach out to me directly. It would be a genuine pleasure for us to bring our live show to as many places as possible and connect with audiences around the world. And as for free time… I think I’ve already had more than enough of that! Now it’s time to get moving, work hard, and give it everything we’ve got. We have a lot of exciting plans ahead, and I can’t wait to see where this new chapter takes us. Hahaha! To wrap things up, I would like to extend my sincere thanks to Bernard for giving us the opportunity to do this interview. It has been a real pleasure to share our thoughts and experiences with you. As always, it is a genuine pleasure have this kind of one-to-one conversation with Side-Line. Thank you for your interest in Mondträume, for your support over the years, and for helping us share our music with your readers. We truly appreciate it. Pikotto. About Mondträume Mondträume is a synthpop project formed in 2010 and based in Spain, built around producer and composer Pikotto. Damasius Venys sang on the early records before leaving in 2020 for Mental Exile. Ivan Derbenev and Madil Hardis worked with the project from 2022, and Nicky Schulschenk took over vocals with the “Heart Machine” EP in December 2023. The line-up is now a duo of Pikotto and Schulschenk. The project has released through Alfa Matrix since its debut, which Side-Line placed among the strongest synthpop albums of the past four decades, and followed with “Lovers, Sinners & Liars”, a record that took five years to complete. The single “Poisoned Love” arrived in December 2024 and was expanded into a digital EP in February 2025, alongside a previous Side-Line interview. The track was later included on Side-Line’s Ukraine charity compilation “United 2 – The Odin Files” in July 2026. Alfa Matrix announced “Mind Games” in April 2026 and released it on 26 June. The 24 tracks split between new songs and remixes, with guest vocals from Madil Hardis on “Immortal”, “Day After Day” and “Whole”, District 13 on “I Tried So Hard” and “Please Don’t Cry”, Neon Space Men on “Heart”, Color Theory on “Better Off” and Antilav on “Falling Snow” and “Something”. The remix side carries reworkings by Code 64, Final Selection, Rob Dust, Beyond Border and Neon Space Men, plus the Mondträume remix of Bruderschaft’s “Falling”. The Leeds and Madrid dates in early 2027 will be the project’s first live shows.

items.body: Most of these songs have been sitting on Bandcamp one at a time since 2020. Music for the basses, the first Xavier Monax album to reach streaming services, brings twelve of them together and runs 42 minutes. The French solo project, which works under the lower-case name monax, describes the record as melancholic material in an indie rock and post-punk style. It went up on Spotify, Apple Music and Deezer on 30 August 2026; the artist gives 18 September as the date it lands on all platforms. The running order is “The Call”, “Is it the stars”, “White rooms”, “14 off”, “Don’t shoot the pianist”, “Leaving the darkness”, “Quiet again”, “Ordinary Fields”, “Follow me”, “Back in town”, “The sound from my mind” and “From here”. Every track had already appeared as a standalone Bandcamp release between November 2020 and April 2026, so the album works as a first collected edition rather than a set of new recordings. It is self-released, with no label and no distributor beyond digital delivery. How the twelve tracks were made Monax plays everything. The credit lines across the catalogue are consistent and terse – “all instruments by monax”, “all musics, Lyrics and instruments by monax” – and the sole exception on this album is “Simon”, where the lyrics are credited to M. Simon. That track is not on “Music for the basses”, but it shows the pattern: one person recording alone, with an outside contribution named when there is one. No producer, mixing or mastering credit is published for the album, and there is no cover-art credit. There are no music videos. The twelve pieces on YouTube are auto-generated art tracks supplied by the distributor, not clips. About Xavier Monax Xavier Monax is a solo project from France. The Bandcamp page gives the country and nothing more precise; there is no city, no biography text and no listed website or social account. Releases are billed as Xavier Monax on streaming services and credited to monax in the liner text. The Bandcamp catalogue is the fuller picture: around 37 items, mixing short albums with a long run of individual tracks. The earliest, “tout est à vendre”, carries a 2003 date. “The John Room Innocence” followed in September 2020 and the single “Music for the Basses” – one track, “Don’t shoot the pianist” – in November 2020. The nine-track “Viral Kiss” arrived in June 2022, “DREAMS 23” in April 2023 and the two-track “Sur le sable” in April 2025. Between those, singles appeared at a steady rate: “The Sound Of My Mind” in October 2022, “14 off” in February 2023, then “Back in town”, “Ordinary Fields”, “Refuges”, “Simon”, “White rooms”, “Follow me” and “Leaving the darkness” across 2024, “From Here” and “Quiet Again” in 2025, and “L’ironie du sort” and “Is it the stars” in 2026. Cover versions of Johnny Cash’s “Hurt” and of Tristana sit alongside them. The project tags its own work as alternative, alternative rock and wave, and has no recorded label history, no announced live dates and no press coverage in any language before now. “Music for the basses” is the first Xavier Monax release to appear outside Bandcamp.

items.body: A reel-to-reel tape sat unplayed for 36 years. On 30 September 2026 the London archival label Nausea Records issues Etiquette Session: 1990, eight songs the Belgian post-punk band Your Eyes recorded in a single day in April 1990 and never released. The band split shortly afterwards. The digital version went up in August; the vinyl is a 45 RPM LP, limited to 200 copies on transparent purple with a lyrics and biography insert. YOUR EYES – Etiquette Session: 1990 LP (NR018) by Nausea Records The record runs “Mein Untergang”, “Looking Through Your Eyes”, “Wouldn’t It Be Great” and “But Still” on the first side, and “As Easy As Hate”, “Dulce Et Decorum Est”, “The Dreamless Sleep” and “Dialogue” on the second. Nico de Haan produced the session at Etiquette Studio in Zandvliet on 16 April 1990. Dutch Tape Transfers restored the master tape in 2025 and Frank Gorissen remastered it at Subterra Recordings from the original reel. Caio Batata laid out the artwork around a Steve Slingeneyer drawing originally made for the promo tape that never appeared, with back-cover photographs by Gerry Smet. Who Your Eyes were The label tells the band’s history plainly: “In 1989, four musicians from Belgium came together with a shared passion for dark, atmospheric post-punk. Inspired by Joy Division, Sisters of Mercy, and the adventurous sounds coming from the 4AD label.” The line-up was Koen Apers on vocals, Kris De Potter on bass, Tom De Dobbelaer on drums and Bart Verlent on guitar, all from Beveren in East Flanders. Within months of forming they had a set together and made their live debut in Antwerp, opening for Enema Joe at a Creatures Of The Night party. The response pushed them into the studio the following spring. Then it ended: De Dobbelaer left soon after the session, and the remaining three played one last show in Beveren with Jan Dhooge behind the kit before calling it off. According to the label, “The reel to reel tape was shelved and the recordings remained unreleased for the next 36 years.” Verlent went on to Sin of Sins, Kandinsky and Hydrom Line, the last of which released through the Belgian label Wool-E Discs in 2000 and again in 2021. He brought the Your Eyes tape to Side-Line’s attention himself. About Nausea Records Nausea Records is a London label run by Marcus Lombardi that describes itself as “A London-based archival label uncovering lost and overlooked punk, post-punk and DIY recordings from the 70s and 80s.” Its catalogue works through unreleased and long-out-of-print European material, with recent titles including Intensified Chaos’ “That’s not Freedom 1982”, T-Red’s “Partie 1984-1985” and Cruel Maniax’ “Atomkrig 1985-1988”. Its other current release is Danza Morta’s “Dead Dance 1985”, issued alongside the Your Eyes LP. The Your Eyes record is the label’s first Belgian title. Vinyl copies are on pre-order through the label’s own store, with the digital version already on Spotify and YouTube. Neither the band nor the label has announced any live activity around the release.

items.body: Djinn & Tone Inc, the electronic project of Fribourg-based musician Mathias Läubli, released The Prince of Darkness on 28 August 2026. The 3:57 track is self-released and sits between synthpop, dance-pop and alternative electronics, with a female vocal carrying a scene set in a fetish club at two in the morning. Läubli filed it under “Dark Electro Pop” on his own SoundCloud, where the description reads “A seductive female vocal relaying the atmosphere in a fetish club at 2am”. Läubli is credited as the composer. He says he wrote, produced and engineered the track himself, and that he dedicated it to a friend who runs sex-positive club nights in Switzerland. No vocalist is credited on Spotify, Apple Music, Deezer or SoundCloud, and the release carries no featured-artist billing – unlike two earlier Djinn & Tone Inc singles, which name Fanny Corboz in the title. The single is on Spotify, Apple Music, Deezer and SoundCloud. It is not on Bandcamp, where the project’s page holds only the 2020 track “Petit Génie”. A Swiss project back in motion after four quiet years “The Prince of Darkness” is the fourth Djinn & Tone Inc single of 2026 and the seventh overall. The catalogue opened on 18 December 2020 with “Petit Génie”, featuring Fanny Corboz and Michael Déforné, then continued with “House Arrest” on 18 February 2022 and “Tibetan Lament”, again with Corboz, on 31 March 2022. Nothing followed for almost four years. The project resumed on 4 January 2026 with “The Climate These Days”, the only release credited to Mathias Läubli rather than the project name, and carried on with “indigo Daze” on 23 January and “Swipe Right” on 3 July. Läubli contacted Side-Line directly, writing that he was “looking for places that still cover new dark electronic music directly rather than through a paid submission platform”. About Djinn & Tone Inc Djinn & Tone Inc is the independent electronic project of Mathias Läubli, who works from Fribourg, Switzerland, and describes himself as a former London resident. He writes, produces and engineers the material himself, and the project has released everything to date without a label, through digital distribution under its own name. In his own account of the project’s range, it “moves between song-based electronic music, pop experiments, guitar-driven grooves and live no-tempo sound work”. He keeps a second strand under the name Djinn Fizz, which he describes as “the quieter, ritual side of the same project” – Tibetan bowls, drones and improvised atmospheric pieces. Djinn Fizz material stays on SoundCloud and has not been issued commercially. The first release, “Petit Génie”, came out of a 2020 collaboration with a musician who wanted something, in Läubli’s words, “Floydesque but with modern sounds”. He brought in Fanny Corboz, a singer he had worked with in an earlier band, for the vocal parts. Michael Déforné, also credited on that release, is the name of a record and hi-fi shop in Fribourg whose owner is a long-standing drummer. Corboz returned for “Tibetan Lament” in 2022. Neither singer is credited on “The Prince of Darkness”, which is Läubli’s first release aimed squarely at the dark electronic scene.

Inglês sings and plays keyboards, and works with Vairinhos in Wildnorthe as well. He composes and records the material; she writes and performs the vocals; the lyrics are credited jointly to Necrø. Their most recent release is the single “Hanged Man”, out on 6 March 2026. The September dates are their first European run since that single.

PHACE)”, with French lyrics delivered half-spoken over synthpop, EBM and techno rhythms. The remix single is the duo’s second release of 2026. items.body: The shoot took Freakangel into a Tallinn dungeon and a pole dance studio. The Estonian industrial rock act premiere the official video for Control on 4 September 2026 at 11:00 CEST, six days before they open a three-country Baltic tour with Psycholies and Sugar Rody. A teaser went up on 31 August. “Control” is the closing part of a trilogy the band built with Alfa Matrix across three years, and it turns slower and more introspective than the two singles before it. Control EP by FREAKANGEL D. Darling produced and directed the video and cut it from two separate shoots. The Freakangel footage was filmed at Kultus Club, a members-only kink venue in Tallinn, with Alex Troitsky as director of photography. The pole dance sequence features Daria Khudinskaia and was filmed by Šilanda Sirakova at Hudi Dance Studio. The band describe the result as built on mood rather than plot: “Rather than following a traditional storyline, the video focuses on atmosphere, movement and the tension between attraction, control and vulnerability.” The song deals with obsession, idealisation and the collapse of an illusion the protagonist built himself. D. Darling and Ocean Black wrote the lyrics and wrote, produced and recorded the track together. Ocean Black has produced every part of the trilogy: “Suicidal (Break The Cycle)” in 2023, “Death Bloom” in 2024 and “Control” in 2026. Alfa Matrix collected all three on the digital “Control” EP on 10 April 2026, then issued the seven-track “Control (Extended)” EP on 26 June 2026 with remixes by Psycholies, PashaRav, Spankthenun and Implant. Freakangel Baltic tour dates with Psycholies and Sugar Rody Psycholies, the Bari goth-industrial act led by Vigos von Lies, also remixed “Control” for the extended edition. Sugar Rody is a Tallinn producer and DJ and a co-founder of the Dark Disko night. 10 September 2026 – Kaunas, Lithuania – Klubas Lemmy 11 September 2026 – Riga, Latvia – Klubs Depo 12 September 2026 – Tallinn, Estonia – The Krypt Freakangel add a fourth September date: 27 September at the Renaissance Alternative Music Festival at Venue 229 in London. Earlier in 2026 the band played Wave-Gotik-Treffen in Leipzig on 22 May, the Tallinn Industrial Festival in April and Hard Rock Laager in Vana-Vigala in July. About Freakangel Freakangel formed in Tallinn, Estonia, in late 2009, started by Dmitry Ivanov, who works as D. Darling, as an offshoot of his other band Suicidal Romance. The project began as an EBM and industrial outfit and moved towards industrial rock across its first decade. Members credited over the years include Dmitry Ivanov, Roman Demchenko, Artjom Balakshin, Ocean Black and Tanel Könd. The band opened their catalogue in 2010 with the album “The Faults Of Humanity” and the “Digital Deviations” release, both on Alfa Matrix, and followed with “Let It All End” and “Porcelain Doll” in 2012, “The Book Of Violence” and “The Ones To Fall” in 2013, “Into The Fire” in 2014 and “The Show Of Violence” in 2015. “How The Ghost Became” arrived in 2016 and “In The Witch House” in 2017, both on DWA, before “Death Walks With Us” in 2018. Alfa Matrix marked the debut with “The Faults Of Humanity (X Anniversary Edition)” in 2021 and issued the “The Last White Dance” EP in 2022. The current run began with the free download single “Death Bloom” in April 2024, followed by a free “Death Bloom (extended version)” EP in October 2024 and the sixteen-track free compilation “Serenity To The Stars, Beauty To The Broken” in September 2024, released ahead of a USA and Mexico tour that October. The “Control” video closes the trilogy that run produced, and the Baltic dates are the band’s first shows since Hard Rock Laager in July.

items.body: Mike Watt returned his bass part within a day. That track now sits at the centre of “Emotional Plea”, the debut single by Work Crush, the new project of Hudson, New York songwriter Stephen Bluhm. The electropop and disco-leaning single was released on 28 August 2026 and is available on Bandcamp. Bluhm wrote the music and lyrics and handled vocals, guitar and synth. Watt, co-founder of the San Pedro punk band Minutemen, plays bass. Alex Wernquest contributed drums and percussion and shares the recording and mixing credit with Bluhm. The track was recorded and mixed at Basement Floods Records in Catskill, New York, with Watt’s bass recorded at Studio tHUNDERpANTS in San Pedro, California. Jeff Lipton mastered it at Peerless Mastering in Boston, with Costanza Tinti as assistant mastering engineer. Musician and illustrator Steve Teare drew the cover, a child playing with a toy military plane. Emotional Plea by Work Crush Why Work Crush wrote ‘Emotional Plea’ The song is a first for Bluhm, who had not written directly about politics before. He explains what pushed him to it: “With Emotional Plea, I’d never written an overtly political protest song, but I felt I couldn’t ignore in my writing what’s happening around us, with ICE, with Gaza, with the complacency and lack of compassion.” The recording came together faster than his usual pace, and Watt’s involvement is the reason he gives for that. “I usually write slowly, but this came together quickly because I felt it so urgently,” Bluhm said. “Mike Watt is one of the funkiest bass players I know, and I knew he’d be perfect for the song. I’m grateful he agreed. He sent his bass track back within 24 hours. The man works furiously.” Musically the single sets a steady dance rhythm under synthesizers and clipped rhythm guitar, with Bluhm singing in a baritone. He describes the project’s method in one line on its release page: “At Work Crush, we believe all kinds of messages and stories can be told through the fine art of disco.” The same note states that no generative AI was used on the release. About Work Crush and Stephen Bluhm Work Crush is the current project of Stephen Bluhm, a songwriter based in Hudson, in New York’s Hudson Valley. Bluhm began releasing music under his own name, issuing the self-titled album “Stephen Bluhm” on 17 September 2017. “Easter” followed on 14 April 2023. His second full-length, “Out of the Nowhere. Into the Here.”, came out on 19 April 2024, recorded, mixed and produced by Bluhm with guest players including musicians from Bard College’s The Orchestra Now and the Bard Conservatory Orchestra. It is built around strings, horns, flutes, piano and reeds rather than synthesizers. An instrumental version of the album was released alongside it. “Emotional Plea” is his first release since that album and the first under the Work Crush name. It moves him from orchestral chamber pop to a synth and dance-rhythm setting, with two collaborators he has worked with before, Alex Wernquest and Steve Teare, and one new one in Mike Watt. No further Work Crush releases have been announced.

items.body: The whispers in my mind, the echoes of my past, Judgment in the mirror, a reflection that will last. The mind can build a courtroom from almost nothing. A remembered phrase becomes evidence, an old mistake is summoned as a witness, and conscience takes the prosecutor’s table before crossing the room to pronounce sentence from the bench. No counsel appears for the defense, no statute of limitations applies, and every hour spent alone provides another opportunity to reopen the case. On Up Against the Wall, Minsk-based artist Tomorrows Letters turns this internal proceeding into a severe and stylish piece of noir synthpop. The solo project of Kiryl Karotki, Tomorrows Letters enters the song already cornered, facing a tribunal in which the accused, prosecutor, and judge occupy the same body. A low, saxophone-like drone opens the recording before giving way to a mechanized groove. Sparse piano notes land beside Karotki’s controlled vocal, lending each phrase the gravity of sworn testimony. His delivery remains cold and composed, yet there is considerable force beneath that restraint, like silk draped across the song’s dread. Trip-hop menace and industrial textures run through the rhythm, meeting the darker electronic pop associated with Depeche Mode’s 1990s and early-2000s records. The clipped construction also carries the severe elegance of 1980s new wave and minimal synth. When the saxophone returns between verses, it winds through organ-like keys and a low electronic buzz, giving the track the character of a neo-noir jazz performance conducted inside a machine. Karotki’s voice completes the setting, transporting the listener into a room filled with stark light, suspended haze, and hard silhouettes. Every word appears carefully measured, as though an answer given too quickly could become further evidence for the prosecution. The lyrics make this psychological trial explicit. Past mistakes supply the testimony, the mirror preserves the verdict, and the heartbeat keeps time for fear. Within the “courtroom of my soul,” the singer bears every role and pays every toll. By the outro, the narrow line between right and wrong has become another instrument of captivity: “I’m a prisoner of my own mind.” “The song describes a state where your own mind acts as both the prosecutor and the judge in a trial that never ends,” Karotki explains. “It’s about being your own worst enemy, trapped in a loop of self-judgment where conscience acts as a punisher rather than a moral guide.” The single release of Up Against the Wall, the first offering from Karotki’s debut LP set for release this autumn. It is accompanied by an exclusive remix from Karotki’s friends in Nürnberg, marking the first of several guest appearances and collaborations planned for the forthcoming album. The song was mixed and mastered by Nürnberg’s sound engineer, Andrei Bobrovka, while its cover artwork was created by Tomorrows Letters. Tomorrows Letters is a project that operates according to a strict hardware-only philosophy, with Karotki using vintage samplers and unconventional songwriting methods to give it a dusty, tactile character. New Romantic and minimal synth-pop influences provide the foundation, though their historical language is put in the service of present-day psychological estrangement. Across his work, Karotki examines isolation, self-judgment, Jungian ideas concerning the hidden self, maladaptive daydreaming, compulsive creation, and the pursuit of victories that prove empty once attained. items.body: And so, as summer draws to a close and we enter the ever-popular fall season (which affords us the use of the word “autumnal”, which you fucking bet we’ll be working in wherever possible), we also enter the final third of 2026. Of course, needing to get our Year End coverage done and dusted by mid-December means we’ve got roughly three months left of coverage, and the actual determination of what records we liked the most still to come. As always, suggestions of things we’ve overlooked are always welcome, as are your own picks, feel free to toss ’em in the comments below. But of course, this is all a preamble for our most venerable tradition, ye olde Tracks post. Join us won’t you? Creux Lies Pig, “An American Ideal of Beauty” Raymond Watts sure is a busy guy these days. Aside from a massive tour he’s kicking off across North America, the Pig mastermind is following up this year’s enjoyable Hurt People Hurt with a smattering of follow-up EPs. The first of those, from which the track embedded below is taken, is Dirt Box, featuring four new tracks with accompanying remixes by the likes of Stabbing Westward, Combichrist, Cyanotic and Rabbit Junk. Then we’ve got Merciless coming down the pike, a remix EP with cuts by Clock DVA (!!) and Pitchshifter amongst others. I guess you can’t keep a good hog down. Dirt Box by PIG Creux Lies, “Jubilate” Man, but Sacramento’s Creux Lies are keeping us on our toes. The depth and richness of sophomore LP Goodbye Divine has us waiting on a follow-up with bated breath, but the third original track they’ve released over the past couple of years sounds very distinct from its predecessors. Here, they’re in an easily approachable synth dancefloor mode, but the real sauce is in the slowburn approach Ean Elliot Clevenger takes to the vocals which build across its runtime. Jubilate by Creux Lies UNTER STRØM, “Stumbling” UNTER STRØM is the side-project of Alex from LA’s post-punkers Matte Blvck, and while it is a more down the pipe electronic project than its parent band, it’s a far cry from the defacto sound of modern electro-darkwave. Indeed, while the sound of their material is certainly of a more shadowy cast, you’re getting programming and arrangements that refer to more aboveground sounds in the world of progressive house and melodic techno, splitting the difference between those bright club nights and dark underground dancefloors in fine fashion. Between Forms by UNTER STRØM alarm!systemen, “Burn” Don’t let the apparent compositional simplicity of Belgian newcomers alarm!systemen’s approach to melancholy coldwave on this track fool you; there’s a real consideration of colour and harmony here which makes a virtue of modern gear and technique rather than eschewing it for the sage of nostalgia, while shooting a style familiar to fans of any number of early 80s continental acts with a bright and fresh strain of dreampop. alarm!systemen by alarm!systemen Evil Dust, “Sadistic” Some good n’ gnarly lo-fi business from London body music act Evil Dust, whose new LP I Just Want to Fit In is due shortly on the 11th of September. If’n you like some of the stuff that the whole industrialized techno sound was doing, but wish it was, well, more industrial, this might fit the bill; heavily percussive, lots of sample work, and an unruly groove that never quite settles in where you think it will. I JUST WANT TO FIT IN by EVIL DUST Einhänder Aus Stahl, “4 Meter Punch To The Face (Visitor remix)” Speaking of lo-fi body music, the new maxi EP from Einhänder Aus Stahl, the side project of Micheal of Chrome Corps, offers a slew of minimal tracks which strip throwback techno and EBM to their barest skeleton. Throw in a little bit of left-field synth-funk courtesy of Visitor (you probably don’t need us to ID the samples for you) and you have a twitchy, burpy blast of fun. items.body: Band:  Jordsjø | Album: Pestkrønikene | Genre: Progressive rock, Heavy psych | Year: 2026 From: Oslo, Norway | Label: Dying Victims Productions For fans of: Anekdoten, Wobbler, Uriah Heep, Rush Bandcamp This is far from the first time Jordsjø has been featured on this site. They’re among the most prominent names in the flourishing Norwegian prog scene, and their music is usually pretty solid. Their last release, the split LP Kontraster with Breidablik, featured some of their best work ever. What I love about  Jordsjø’s usual work is the way they integrate classic Anglo-prog elements with ample Nordic folk flavors. Pestkrønikene (Eng.: The Plague Chronicles), then, marks something of a break from their usual style. The music here is much heavier, harder, and fuzzier, drawing from classic heavy psych sounds. It’s certainly different from their usual output, but it’s another strong entry in their discography. Pestkrønikene opens with its title track. Dramatic stabs of organ and Mellotron eventually lead into a hazy, murky milieu. Flute helps lend some levity; the sharpness cuts through the thickness of everything else quite nicely. Jordsjø doesn’t completely ditch their folk roots here, with a brief interlude in the second half providing some good contrast. “White Magic” features guest vocals from Jon Henriksen of Norwegian heavy metal band Black Magic. Flavors of 1960s psychedelia are prominent with the dreamy vocals and acoustic backing. Even when crunchier tones come in, they harken back to the late ’60s and early ’70s, as opposed to more modern metal. “Seven Heads” is based around an askew blues riff, and this is simply not one of the best songs on the album. Jordsjø is a talented band that can play a lot of different music quite well, but blues is a genre that feels somewhat clunky coming from them. They (more briefly) dabbled in the blues on the two preceding songs, and those moments were similarly weak in comparison. At least the second half of this song features some fun and exciting instrumental moments. The instrumental “Kaosvelde – Vasallens Elegi” (“Chaos Fields – Vasallen’s Elegy”) is more in Jordsjø’s typical wheelhouse. Flute and acoustic guitar are supported by synth and Mellotron, and this functions as a nice interlude. That is followed by another instrumental, “Kaosveldets Endelikt” (“End of the Chaos Fields”), featuring Lars Fredrik Frøislie of Wobbler on organ. This is the heaviest cut on the album, and it’s also the most convincing Jordsjø has been as a metal band (by 1970s standards).  We get another Wobbler guest feature on “The Awakened”, with Andreas Prestmo providing vocals. This song sees Jordsjø bust out their best Rush impression. The guitar chords are distinctly Lifesonian, and the riffs are complex and muscular. Prestmo’s vocals, as usual, are more evocative of Jon Anderson than Geddy Lee, and this combination helps to keep this cut from being simple Rush-aping. “Spiritual Lament” features drummer Kristian Valbo in a guest appearance, and he makes the most of his time here. Where “The Awakened” felt like a Rush song for its guitar parts, this feels like one for its drumming. Valbo clearly takes a lot of inspiration from Neil Peart, especially in his complex, tom-heavy fills. (There are some quite Rush-y guitar and synth parts on this cut, too.) Jon Henriksen makes one final appearance on this album’s last song, “Talisman II”. This feels the most like a typical Jordsjø song of any piece on this album. There are plenty of obvious tributes to early ’70s hard rock, but the band’s usual prog-folk stylings are prominent throughout. Jordsjø’s foray into hard rock is an interesting experiment. It’s not the band’s best album, but I like it. It’s fun to hear a band paying homage to their influences while also bringing their usual character along.  Score: 74/100

items.body: Februus is the ancient Roman god of putrefaction and cleansing. Symbolically, a figure's fiery dome alludes to rampant mental activity, psychological distress, or enlightenment. The firey-headed two gentlemen on the cover art of Construction of Conflict (illustrated by Daniel Karlsson) are probably undergoing some divine spiritual awakening in the presence of that god. The Swedish one-man progressive death metal act Februus aren't strangers to the concept of the flaming noggin: last year, they released a short EP, The Crushing Pressure of Oppressive Thought, featuring a similarly-suited man with what seems to be his brain floating above him with a trail of flames. But can the project's death metal truly melt one's face?Februus is the work of solo member Andreas Karlsson juggles vocals, guitars, bass, synths, and drum programming—no wonder his head's on fire! He associates with tough-to-play genres, supposedly techdeath blended with progressive metal, but sonically, his artistic choices are questionable. While technically professional, Construction of Conflict is produced incredibly unharmoniously, which would make sense if Karlsson aimed for a dissonant death metal record, which it may as well be. His vocals are echoed close to beyond audibility, and the drums follow suit. Can you fathom how loud everything has to be for the drums—on a progressive/technical death metal album—to be mostly undetectable? Only during thrashy segments like the near-end of "The First Limb is Cut" or, at their fullest, during the jazzy instrumental interlude "The Misery That Awaits the World" can you truly detect the drums, and I'm not as disgruntled as I should be at the fact of their programming, since I can't hear them anyway.I'll reiterate it once more: the guitars on this album are LOUD. Riff-forward instrumentation is key to Februus' style, and the riffs sure are friggin' forward. Karlsson is a guitar maestro, able to both noodle with care (see "Fueled by Narcissism" for a lovely, lengthy solo) and wank around (see the aforementioned song's closer for chiptune-adjacent blasts) concisely, but there are better ways of proving this than with noxiously blaring mixing. On denser compositions like "Measures of Escalation" and "Suppressing the Future," the atmosphere is simply draining because of its overwhelming levels of chugging. Most of these stouter cuts' efforts to ease the conditions by way of a waltzy, guitar-led component or a jazzy break, but the "recorded in an alleyway" effect strips these additions of their supposed relief. I'm sure Karlsson had great intentions with these features, but they can't distract from the glaring production job. These segments are also the only times his bass and synths are tended to; two instruments that could contribute plenty to the record's atmosphere if it weren't for their sonic exclusion. After a solid forty-and-a-half minutes, you'll acclimate to Februus's mixing job, and you may even find it endurable. But beginning the album is quite difficult, and your precious headphones need to be 5% lower than what you think. Otherwise, Andreas Karlsson is going to immolate your brain. Construction of Conflict by FEBRUUS
