items.body: “Singing my songs I hold dear; from my virtual world to yours” – Isekaijoucho Hello there! And welcome to the J-Music Exchange/Rate! If you know exactly what that means and what we’re all about here, you should also be well aware what to do from here on out, so off you go! However, if this is actually your first time here and you’re not entirely sure what you just walked into, please give the following primer a quick read: The Exchange/Rate is a tandem album review series conducted every month by yours truly alongside my good friend and fellow Japanese music fan Al (from Omunibasu). Each month we decide on a specific theme with which our reviews would revolve around. We then pick out albums from our respective libraries which we think best coincides with that theme. We will then give the album we chose to the other person and vice versa (exchange), after which we then listen to and subsequently review the album we were given (rate). This project has not only allowed us to explore music beyond our libraries, but it provides an opportunity for us to see our favorite albums from a different point of view. It is our hope that this series is able to do the same for you and that you either find a new artist to try out and/or we offer you a fresh take on one of *your* favorite albums This month it was my turn again to dish out a theme. I think I came up with a pretty interesting one specifically within the context of the Exchange/Rate. and that is bands/artists we started listening to thanks to the Exchange/Rate! I think when Al and I first started doing this series, the most obvious way of looking at the “exchange” part of the Exchange/Rate was simply through the albums we gave each other. I send him something I think he’d find interesting, he does the same for me, and every month we both hopefully walk away having listened to something we otherwise might not have checked out on our own. But after years of doing this, I think it’s fair to say that the exchange goes quite a bit further than that. We’ve talked about a plethora of artists between the two of us at this point, whether through the albums we’ve directly exchanged, comparisons made during reviews, conversations outside of the series, or simply repeatedly exposing each other to certain names until eventually curiosity gets the better of us. Naturally, some of those artists have stuck around long after their respective Exchange/Rate appearances, becoming part of our regular listening habits in the process. So this month, we thought it’d be fun to look at a couple of those artists and see where that influence has taken us. On my end I went ahead and handed Al Soul/R&B artist MALIYA’s album pluto for him to go over with you guys at the Omunibasu Substack (check it out here!). Al in turn had me revisit the one and only Isekaihoucho’s Shikisai for me to talk about and review. So, without further ado, let us enter Isekaijoucho’s world! ーー Isekaijoucho (ヰ世界情緒) is a Japanese virtual singer affiliated with the artist collective KAMITSUBAKI STUDIO, as well as a member of the virtual singer group Virtual Witch Phenomenon, better known as V.W.P. Described as a “virtual dark singer,” Isekaijoucho aims to express the world through her songs and creative works, often weaving themes of darkness and light together through her distinctively powerful yet ethereal singing voice. Beyond music, she’s also a multifaceted creator who expresses herself through a number of different mediums, including illustration, narration, and voice acting. ＜Ｓｈｉｋｉｓａｉ (色彩)＞(＊Spotify link to the full album) CDJapan Affiliate Link(s):N/A ＜T ｒａｃｋｌｉｓｔ＞ ０１・息吹/ibuki -instrumental-０２・そして白に還る/soshite shiro ni kaeru０３・ラピスのお人形/lapis no oningyou０４・パンドラコール/pandora call０５・ディメンション/dimension０６・キミ消失セカイ/kimi shoushitsu sekai０７・グレイスケイル/grayscale０８・此処に棘と死を/koko ni toge to shi o０９・ネリネの内緒事/nerine no naishogoto１０・暮れなずむ約束/kurenazumu yakusoku１１・ヴァーミリオン/vermillion１２・描き続けた君へ/kaki wo tsudxuketa kimi e１３・かたちなきもの/katachinakimono１４・ANGELIC１５・色彩-instrumental- Ａｌ：I first knew about Isekaijoucho through Leap’s various recommendations, but most prevalently within the Exchange/Rate segment, when I reviewed V.W.P’s first full-length album. And similar to being introduced to a brand new idol group, it was neat to learn about all these different personalities and think about how much KAMITSUBAKI struck digital gold when assembling this vocal superteam. And while I’ve come to really appreciate all of them and what they bring to the unit, Isekaijoucho was the one member that caught my eye the most. Given that visuals are important in the world of virtual talents, I’d imagine that a lot of people, myself included, gravitated towards the cute appeal of her design. But looks can be (somewhat) deceiving, as I quickly realized just how much of a fantastic and nuanced singer she really is. As many have pointed out, Joucho has excelled at performing more operatic songs, adding to the dramatic theatrics through her eeriely calm demeanor and ability to sing to the high heavens when needed. And I do think that her most recent full-length album, Colors, exemplifies that visual/auditory contrast of hers and much more. Songs like “Lapis no Ohitogata” and “Pandora Call” have always stood out to me for its mysterious attractiveness and how it fits Joucho’s personality pretty nicely. But what I found most interesting about this record is her apparent desire to expand her range, as we later hear Joucho perform on tracks that stray a bit farther from her usual stuff. Obviously, you can tell that she holds her own on those heavier rock tracks; but listening to her take on various styles like a jazzy musical number, a touching piano ballad, or even something you’d normally hear Harusaruhi rap on… it’s all an impressive display of who Joucho is as an evolving singer and the heights that she’s very well capable of reaching. I have always had a lot of admiration for faceless talents, as they’ve proven that revealing your real identity is not always a necessity in the world of public/online entertainment. And while I never was really caught up in the massive ‘virtual talent’ wave we’ve been seeing over the years, no doubt has it given people endless ways to express themselves through their pursuits of content creation, gaming, art, and especially music. And with how Joucho has presented herself in this album, it’s hard not to see her as a prime example of that type of creative talent. ＜Ｓｏｎｇｓ ｏｆ Ｉｎｔｅｒｅｓｔ＞ ０１・息吹/Ibuki -instrumental-、０２・そして白に還る/soshite shiro ni kaeruI do find it a little funny that this is now the second album in a row we’ve reviewed here on the Exchange/Rate that begins with a dedicated instrumental opener (lol). For what it’s worth though, and as I mentioned last month, I actually enjoy these quite a bit when they’re used to lead directly into the first proper song on an album, which is once again the case here with Ibuki and Soshite Shiro ni Kaeru. Ibuki opens with this grand choir hymn that immediately gives the album an almost mystical, high-fantasy feel. That imagery only becomes stronger as the orchestral accompaniment gradually comes into view, complete with sweeping strings and blaring horns that make it feel as though we’re standing at the beginning of some grand hero’s adventure. It’s brief, but it does exactly what I would want an opening instrumental like this to do; set the scene before seamlessly handing things off to what comes next. Fittingly enough, the choir then gives way to Isekaijoucho’s own beautiful hymn at the beginning of Soshite Shiro ni Kaeru. And I think it’s at around this point that anyone who isn’t terribly familiar with Joucho, or perhaps only knows her through some of the covers she’s done over the years, might start to realize that she’s actually a bit of a singing virtuoso. I don’t just mean that in the sense that she has a good voice either. I personally think she does, of course, though I can also understand her particular tonality perhaps being an acquired taste for some. What impresses me more is the sheer amount of control she has over it. There’s an almost uncanny precision to the way she moves between notes, adjusts the weight behind her voice, and knows exactly how much of it to use at any given moment. I honestly wouldn’t be surprised to learn that she’s had some form of classical training in the past, though I’d probably be even more impressed if she hasn’t. There’s just this innate sense of grandeur to the way she sings that makes performances like this feel remarkably natural for her. You get a pretty good sense of all of that listening to Soshite Shiro ni Kaeru, which, in my opinion, is Isekaijoucho very much in her element. Give Joucho a huge instrumental arrangement and enough room to make use of the technical range at her disposal, and she has an incredible ability to rise right alongside it rather than getting swallowed up by everything happening around her; a dynamic that I’ve always found particularly fascinating about her music. ０７・グレイスケイル/grayscaleWhich is kinda funny when you then arrive at Grayscale around the midway point of the album, as it sounds almost nothing like Soshite Shiro ni Kaeru. This is, of course, very much by design, as I’m sure a lot of you have probably clued in on as well. I’ll talk a little more later about what I think Grayscale represents within the broader context of Shikisai, but to give you guys a bit of a hint, it does dovetail into both the visual and auditory narrative that the album appears to be building. At the very least, I don’t think its placement here is simply for the sake of giving listeners a breather before heading into the album’s latter half. Going back to the song itself though, if I’m being completely honest, I didn’t really know what to make of it during my first couple of spins through the album. Initially, I mostly chalked it up to some of KAMITSUBAKI’s broader musical tendencies bleeding into Isekaijoucho’s own work, given the group’s penchant for electronic music and rap, both of which I’m also a fan of. After a while though, Grayscale started tickling a part of my brain that I haven’t really ventured into for the longest time. The more I listened to it, the more it began reminding me of an artist I listened to a ton when I was first getting into Japanese music; specifically, old-school DAOKO from her indie days under LOW HIGH WHO? There’s something about the quick, almost spoken-word style of rap that Joucho employs here that takes me back to that period of DAOKO’s music, where her delivery would almost casually tumble across the beat rather than approaching it like a more conventional rap performance. And I think that’s what ultimately got me to appreciate Grayscale quite a bit more than I initially did. Her youthful voice and demeanor aside, Isekaijoucho has always struck me as a consummate professional through and through. A track like this takes her considerably further away from the grand, technically demanding vocal performances that I personally associate with her, yet she never comes across as uncomfortable doing it. If anything, I thought she acquitted herself remarkably well, adapting her delivery to what the song asks of her without making it feel like she’s merely trying on a style for novelty’s sake. It’s certainly not the version of Isekaijoucho I expected to hear after the way Shikisai begins, but given what the album is seemingly trying to accomplish, I have a feeling that’s precisely the point. ０８・此処に棘と死を/koko ni toge to shi woThis middle portion of Shikisai is actually my favorite stretch of the album to go through. Not only does it provide a nice stylistic shakeup around the halfway point, but I also think it makes for just about the best demonstration of Isekaijoucho’s versatility as a singer. You really only have to look at the jump from Grayscale to Koko ni Toge to Shi wo to see what I mean. Circling back to something I mentioned at the very beginning, Joucho, in my opinion, is truly right at home performing against these big, theatrical orchestral arrangements. There’s almost a Broadway-esque quality to her delivery here, particularly in the way she’s able to rise to meet the scale and drama of the instrumentation around her. And again, I think part of why this works so well comes from the contrast inherent to Isekaijoucho herself. If you were to hear her speaking voice or even just look at her character design, you probably wouldn’t immediately expect this kind of performance from her. Her voice naturally comes across as incredibly dainty and fragile, and I’ll even concede that there are singers out there with stronger natural vocal qualities than her. But that’s where I think the distinction between having a great voice and being a great singer becomes incredibly important. Because whatever Joucho might lack in natural vocal power, she more than makes up for through sheer technique. That’s perhaps my favorite thing about her as a performer. As delicate as she might look and sound, at no point does Isekaijoucho ever truly feel outsized by the music around her. You can put these massive strings, pounding percussion, and all sorts of theatrical flourishes behind her, and somehow she always finds a way to make herself feel every bit as important to the arrangement. Of course, credit for that doesn’t belong solely to Joucho. Vocaloid producer SLAVE.V-V-R, making their sole contribution to Shikisai here, gives her one hell of a composition to work with. More broadly though, I also have to give KAMITSUBAKI STUDIO a lot of credit for seemingly understanding exactly what makes Isekaijoucho such an interesting vocalist and continually putting her in musical situations where those qualities can shine. １２・描き続けた君へ/kaki tsudzuketa kimi eIn my initial draft for this review, I thought I was gonna have a hard time deciding on one final song to feature before giving my overall impressions on the album. But after giving Shikisai a fair number of spins, I eventually realized that I couldn’t bring myself not to cap everything off with Kaki Tsudzuketa Kimi e. For one, in as much as I really enjoy the theatrical presentation of something like Koko ni Toge to Shi wo, part of me believes that this kind of electro chamber pop arrangement is where Isekaijoucho could ultimately find a lot of mainstream success. There’s this grand, almost epic quality to the song that I could very easily imagine translating to a big game or anime tie-up, while still retaining enough of the characteristics that make Joucho’s music feel distinctly her own. More importantly for this review though, I also think Kaki Tsudzuketa Kimi e serves as a perfectly positioned capstone performance for just about everything we’ve talked about thus far regarding Joucho’s prowess as a singer. While I’d probably still say Koko ni Toge to Shi wo is my favorite song off Shikisai as a whole, the stretch from around 3:23 through the end of Kaki Tsudzuketa Kimi e might just be my favorite sequence on the entire album. Everything about it is just gorgeous. I love how quickly the melody moves and evolves over such a short span of time, constantly giving Joucho something new to respond to as the arrangement builds toward its conclusion. And respond she does, because she absolutely steals the show here. After an entire album spent demonstrating just how much control she has over her voice, Joucho finally gets this extended vocal run where it feels like she’s letting everything loose at once. It’s become one of those moments that I actively look forward to whenever I put the song on. ＜Ｗｈａｔ Ｉ ｔｈｉｎｋ ｏｆ Ｓｈｉｋｉｓａｉ ＞ If you’re a longtime reader of the blog and follower of the Exchange/Rate series, then you should already be well familiar with the term “grab bag”. As a quick refresher, a “grab bag” is what Al and I have taken to calling albums that showcase a number of different musical styles, as opposed to something more uniform that’s built predominantly around a singular style or sound signature. Over the years since we first started using the term, we’ve revisited the concept across a number of different reviews, attempting to further define not only what makes an album a grab bag, but also why an artist might choose to make one and, perhaps more importantly, who exactly they’re meant for. It’s quite honestly become one of my favorite recurring concepts to revisit as part of the Exchange/Rate. Mostly because, as much as Al and I have talked about grab bags over the years, our understanding of them continues to evolve as we encounter albums that approach the idea in different ways. And wouldn’t you know it, we’re gonna be doing that again here with Isekaijoucho’s Shikisai. Shikisai translates rather simply to “colors,” specifically referring to color as we perceive it through light and its different wavelengths. With that in mind, something I find immediately interesting about the album, and something you’ve probably already noticed just by looking at its artwork, is that despite what a title like Shikisai might lead you to expect, the album itself isn’t something I would necessarily describe as colorful. If anything, it’s overwhelmingly white. But that’s also where I think the conceptual brilliance of Shikisai starts to reveal itself, because white isn’t actually the absence of color. Rather, when we’re talking about light, white is what we perceive when all of its different colors come together. And suddenly, the way Shikisai sounds begins to make a whole lot more sense. Because make no mistake, Shikisai is absolutely a grab bag. Across the album, you can hear Isekaijoucho moving between grand orchestral compositions, electronic music, rap, chamber pop, and plenty of other ideas in between. On the surface, these can seem like wildly different directions for the same album to take. Like, we only have to look back at Grayscale immediately followed by Koko ni Toge to Shi wo to see just how dramatic those differences can become. But I don’t think those differences are incidental. I think they’re the entire point. Each style effectively becomes another color for Isekaijoucho to inhabit. Taken individually, they’re all distinct from one another, sometimes drastically so. Bring all of them together, however, and they begin to form the white that defines Shikisai visually. The one constant holding all of those colors together, of course, is Joucho herself, who is appropriately clad in white. ＜Ｍｙ Ｒａｔｉｎｇ＞４.５ ｏｕｔ ｏｆ ５ ＆ ９ ｏｕｔ ｏｆ １０ Which brings me back to why I’ve spent so much of this review talking about her ability as a singer. Whether you give her something theatrical and orchestral like Soshite Shiro ni Kaeru or Koko ni Toge to Shi wo, ask her to rap on something as comparatively unconventional as Grayscale, or give her the soaring electro chamber pop of Kaki Tsudzuketa Kimi e, Isekaijoucho continually finds a way to adapt herself to whatever the composition asks of her. And I think that’s ultimately the biggest takeaway we’re meant to have from Shikisai. Not necessarily that Isekaijoucho has the greatest voice you’ll ever hear, because as I’ve mentioned throughout this review, that’s not really the argument I’m trying to make. Rather, what makes Joucho such an exceptional vocalist is what she’s capable of doing with that voice. Technique, control, adaptability, and an almost uncanny ability to understand what a song needs from her; throw just about any color at Isekaijoucho and she’ll find some way to make it hers. ーー What are your guys’ thoughts on Isekaijoucho’s Shikisai? Let us know in the comments! Likewise, if there are any bands or artists you started listening to thanks to the Exchange/Rate over the years, please share those with us too! We’d love to know! Lastly, before I let you guys go, don’t forget to check out Al’s review of pluto by MALIYA over at the Omunibasu Substack if you haven’t yet! Happy Listening!

items.body: Dana Vynnytska ordered an Indian harmonium, a keyboard worked by a hand-pumped bellows, at a point when she’d just started to see light again after a hard stretch, and sat with the instrument alone until melodies began to surface. What came out of those sessions became “Będę Szczęśliwa” (“I Will Be Happy”), the first single from DAGADANA‘s sixth studio album, Lumen. DAGADANA is built around Vynnytska and Daga Gregorowicz, a Polish and Ukrainian duo who write and sing in both languages, once Bartosz Nazaruk wrapped an afro-funk-inspired beat around Vynnytska’s chords and Mikołaj Pospieszalski slid a bass line underneath. Polish and Ukrainian verses trade off across “Będę Szczęśliwa,” each one answering the other, both circling back to the same picture of a river, all bends and sudden current, and a woman learning to swim with it instead of fighting it. “Gdy odpuszczam jestem kołem. Uratuję nas oboje,” Vynnytska sings at the turn of the song, “When I let go, I become the wheel. I’ll save us both,” a line she wrote out of her own experience of forgiving, herself first, then somebody else, to find her way back to that light. Gregorowicz puts it even simpler: happiness starts the moment you drop a grudge instead of carrying it around. That’s a long way from where DAGADANA started, back in 2006, when Gregorowicz and Vynnytska met at a jazz workshop in Kraków and began singing together before either of them had a band name for it. Pospieszalski and Nazaruk joined not long after, and the four of them have spent eighteen years since turning that meeting into a Fryderyk, Poland’s top music industry award, festival stages from Glastonbury to Oslo World, tours through 34 countries that took them from the Moroccan desert to Beijing’s Forbidden City, and “Jesień, Tańcuj,” the song they co-wrote for the Oscar-nominated film Chłopi. “Będę Szczęśliwa” is pulled from Lumen, Latin for light, their sixth studio album, still without a confirmed release date. The band has said it’s a step away from the folk sound that built their name. Pospieszalski produced the single himself; Mateusz Hulbój mixed it and Rafał Smoleń mastered it. Sandra Matyszewska shot and directed the video alongside Gregorowicz and Vynnytska, at Folwark Konny Hermanów, a horse farm on the Warta River in western Poland. items.body: Honoring its title, Justyna Jablonska‘s Unforeseen never heads exactly where expected; in fact, it’s not even close. The cellist’s debut solo album drips with the confidence of exploration, incorporating multiple genres while acting as a metaphor for the immigrant experience. Jablonska connects the migration of birds with the migration of people and the migration of oft-improvised notes, focusing on the lives of Ukrainian, Polish and Roma Gypsy migrants. While this seems like a lot to tackle, the artist does so with aplomb. The album begins as one might expect a cellist’s album to begin, with sedate phrasing, multitracked lines and a regal tone. The title track demonstrates Jablonska’s depth of emotion while establishing the baseline from which it will soon wander. Were the record to have continued in this vein, it would have remained exemplary; yet the artist strives for something greater, just as those dreaming for a better life might pack their belongings, imitating the flocks passing overhead in the spring and fall. As “If You Can Hear This” launches with a spoken word sample and jungle rhythms, all bets are off. The artist will not be confined by expectation. Is it safe? Not at all, and therein lies the appeal. The bird, the immigrant, the artist may each be called upon to adapt to new surroundings. “9 Daughers” is the first of three vocal pieces, beginning in birdsong and proceeding to a rendition of a traditional Lithuanian folk song A linden tree has nine branches, each one corresponding to a daughter, who each in turn are married, leaving the mother to “sweep the ashes.” The tone is one of mingled celebration and sadness: the empty nest, the broken tree. Can even the birds sing the sorrow away? The next piece starts with the sound of traffic, implying movement; then peaceful kalimba, cello and electronics, each in turn moving the music further away from its origins. The skies open in “Wayward,” and Jablonska seems forlorn, until a series of upbeat melodies are translated to percussion and string. These are the unforeseen joys of leaving the place where one has begun; by the end, the skies have cleared. But not all changes are easy; “Fabryka” introduces a brief note of dissonance, setting the listener up for Monika Niemczynowicz’s return on “The Pact,” an extremely dark cautionary tale from Roztocze, Poland. The presence of such songs underlines the connection between land, culture and memory ~ tales passed down generation to generation, even when the family has migrated to a new home. One hungers for the live show, incorporating film and copious amounts of spoken word, hinted at in the final minute of “Procession.” The album’s greatest surprise arrives toward the end with “Shchedryk (feat. Sofiia Fylypiv).” Most listeners will recognize “Carol of the Bells” in an instant, and many will recall its Ukrainian origins, but few will remember that the song predates Christianity and is about a swallow wishing a family “prosperity, good fortune and a fruitful year.” Jablonska reinstates the original title and meaning, reclaiming it from distortion. This too is a metaphor for the immigrant experience: the temptation to integrate to the extent that one’s history is sublimated. Jablonska, who lives in Glasgow, closes with her own take on “The Skye Boat Song,” which was itself adapted from a Gaelic tune. By the end, one is wondering about the the tug between one’s national origin and country of residence, and the very definition of home. (Richard Allen)

items.body: A label and collective that kept going, kept releasing, kept refining a shared aesthetic without compromise or concession to trends. aux4444 pt.1 carries all of that history in its drum patterns and melodic builds, and it sounds better for it. This is what underground electronic music looks like when it’s done with genuine conviction over a sustained period of time. Fusing IDM and nostalgia that also carries significant electro elements aux4444 pt.1 by omni causa   mind​color​music is a Berlin-based label that has been operating quietly and consistently since 2009 (and previously as a party series), building a catalog of braindance, IDM, jungle, and breakbeat electronica across limited hand-stamped physical releases and digital editions. The label’s naming scheme immediately stands out—every release carries the “aux” prefix followed by a number, a system that applies across all artists on the roster and functions as a unified catalog language rather than individual release titles. aux44 is the name of the series—44 stands for the precinct number of the Berlin Neukölln borough. It’s a clean, distinctive approach that signals something about how the label thinks about its output, not as a collection of individual artist statements but as a continuous ongoing archive (connected to their location) of a shared aesthetic community. The numbers aren’t just catalog codes; they’re evidence of continuity, of a project that has been running long enough to reach four-digit entries. Once you notice it, it catches the eye immediately. ​omni causa—the Berlin-based producer at the center of the mindcolormusic collective, has been releasing material on the label since its earliest releases, with collaborations alongside tysk raider (as Omnibusraider), microlith, fah, and foreign sequence building a catalog that sits consistently in braindance and IDM territory without ever leaning i​nto the acid-heavy, distortion-forward side of the genre. This is melodic and beat-driven braind​ance, loops, breaks, and emotional structure rather than squelching 303 work. aux4444 pt.1 collects material recorded between January 2021 and September 2024, a three-year span tha​t gives the release a sense of accumulated thought rather than a single session document. “Its Relative” is the standout, the most ambitious track on the release in terms of rhythm and structure. The drums carry it entirely. Distorted kicks and a percussion loop hitting in detuned rhythm with what sounds like broken ring modulation applied create a genuinely compelling effect. The melodic builds surrounding that rhythmic core are well placed, surfacing and receding without competing for space. “Perspectives,” the track that follows, is a happy braindance-ish piece where the drum rhythms and bassline work together as something genuinely catchy. The pads build in a way that’s consistent across the album but lands particularly well here. It has a structural and melodic familiarity that recalls how Cylob organized composition on Cylobian Sunset (1996), not in sound, nowhere near what Cylob produces aesthetically, but in the way melody is laid out and the builds are sequenced. That compositional logic, that familiar approach to developing a braindance track from its initial statement toward something larger, is recognizable here and executed with real confidence. The drum work throughout is the album’s strongest consistent element. Break samples fused with analog drum sounds and what sounds like custom electronic percussions tampered enough to matter, it’s a good fusion of IDM and nostalgia that also carries significant electro elements throughout. That electro thread connects aux4444 pt.1 to a lineage of melodic, beat-focused IDM that ran through the Toytronic label in the early 2000s, artists like Multiplex‘s adjacent work, Gimmik‘s more accessible moments, and producers like Bochum Welt, whose warmth and melodic intelligence sat somewhere between electro and IDM without fully committing to either. mindcolormusic has been doing this long enough that reaching the 44 mark in its catalog numbering feels less like a milestone and more like evidence of something quietly remarkable: a label and collective that kept going, kept releasing, kept refining a shared aesthetic without compromise or concession to trends. aux4444 pt.1 carries all of that history in its drum patterns and melodic builds, and it sounds better for it. This is what underground electronic music looks like when it’s done with genuine conviction over a sustained period of time. aux4444 pt.1 is available on mindcolormusic. items.body: On Islands Alight, percussion takes on a structural role, the bass gains weight, echo intervenes in the form, and the pulse alters the relationship between the different parts. The British composer points to the history of dub within electronic music as one of the project’s sources. Entrusting rhythm with a greater share of the tension Islands Alight by James Murray   James Murray arrives at this work after a path in which restraint has become an aesthetic choice even before a technical one. For years, his electronic music has pursued a precise relationship between duration, timbre, and memory. He favors slow construction, minimal variation, and change that acquires meaning over time. The new album brings this approach into more rhythmic territory, shifting the center of gravity of his writing. The transition feels significant precisely because of how naturally it occurs. Murray has long worked with minimal electronic and electroacoustic forms, dense with detail and shaped by a strong awareness of sound. On Islands Alight, percussion takes on a structural role, the bass gains weight, echo intervenes in the form, and the pulse alters the relationship between the different parts. The British composer points to the history of dub within electronic music as one of the project’s sources. It is the most appropriate reference through which to understand this aspect of the album: a culture of space, listening, and studio transformation absorbed into a personal body of research. Four years of work have produced a cohesive record. Continuity is one of its greatest strengths. The London-based musician prefers to work with relationships, allowing an element to change function through what surrounds it. A rhythmic figure gains incisiveness through a minimal shift. A harmonic sequence recedes, allowing a previously secondary detail to emerge. The control is rigorous and almost always discreet. This economy is part of his poetics. Murray places value on restraint, listening, attention to detail, and trust in the person receiving the music. Islands Alight translates these principles into a very concrete form. Passages are given the time they need to develop their function. Resolutions are postponed. Gratification often arrives only after an extended period within the same sonic field, once the relationship between the elements has already altered perception. “Echo alters the memory of what has just happened. Low frequencies establish weight and continuity. Percussion introduces pressure. The synthesizers retain the emotional quality that has long characterized his work. Together, these elements produce music that remains unmistakably his.” ~Mirco Salvadori Rhythm changes this dynamic considerably. It introduces a more pronounced physical dimension and makes the music more mobile. Percussion guides the listening experience with an elastic presence. The pulse moves forward, thins out, then returns with a different weight. Bass affects both depth and the perception of time. Delay and reverb organise distance, duration, and density. The effects belong to the composition just as much as the harmonic parts do. The relationship with the history of dub can be measured above all through this method. Murray takes certain production principles and brings them into his own language. The studio becomes part of the writing process. Echo alters the memory of what has just happened. Low frequencies establish weight and continuity. Percussion introduces pressure. The synthesizers retain the emotional quality that has long characterized his work. Together, these elements produce music that remains unmistakably his. Islands Alight retains a strong connection with his recent history. Weeds had already demonstrated how detail could become structure and how limited variation could acquire emotional significance. His work with Ian Hawgood confirmed his ability to treat sonic material with extreme patience. The new record introduces a different kind of mobility. The writing appears more sensitive to weight, entrusting rhythm with a greater share of the tension. The environmental theme identified by the artist also enters into this perspective. Murray has linked the record to heatwaves, drought, and a form of ecological anxiety connected to the present. These references operate as an internal pressure within the project. The titles evoke waters, islands, calms, marine animals, and currents. They provide essential coordinates while keeping meaning open. The music proceeds according to its own logic, allowing those images to operate at a deeper level. Murray builds tension using limited means :: The cover follows the same sense of restraint. The original photograph is transformed until color, material, and folds become its dominant features. With only a few elements, the image suggests change and fragility. Its connection with the record is immediate precisely because of its sobriety. The most interesting quality of this album lies in the way Murray manages continuity. Duration makes minute transformations perceptible. The music demands concentration, yet soon reveals a very clear internal scale. A detail that initially seems marginal can acquire prominence several minutes later. A pulse can change its function through a simple shift in context. In this way, Murray builds tension using limited means. Melody retains a decisive role. The harmonies possess the controlled melancholy already present in his previous work, but here they are exposed differently to rhythm, bass, and effects. The production follows the same principle. Definition is high, the detail carefully handled, and depth meticulously managed. The technical work maintains an evident musical function. Murray uses control to give the individual elements autonomy and to make small differences in weight and intensity perceptible. Even in the densest passages, the sound remains clear and readable. Such rigorous control also entails an element of risk. Some passages display a highly regulated timbral continuity, leaving less room for the unexpected. Yet this choice is entirely consistent with the character of a record that demands time and a willingness to engage with slowness. Its idea of movement develops through persistence and internal variation. Some listeners may find this discipline severe. It is also the point at which James Murray expresses his concept of composition most clearly. Trust in the listener therefore becomes central. The record offers few explicit signals and allows meaning to emerge through duration. Some elements gain importance when they disappear. Others appear almost motionless, yet change their function through a new rhythmic relationship. Complexity presents itself with great discretion. Complexity presents itself with great discretion :: This makes Islands Alight a significant work within Murray’s discography. It brings together melodic sensitivity, an interest in electroacoustic material, precision in sound design, and a rhythmic investigation developed with particular depth. The influence of dub history expands the tools at his disposal and shapes his treatment of space, pulse, and the studio. The ambient dimension continues to inform his sensibility, in keeping with the open and undogmatic definition Murray himself has always preferred for his music. The result possesses a particular strength because it avoids the need to announce its change. Islands Alight works as an internal development. Elements that have long been present find a different proportion and produce new consequences. Murray knows his own language well and modifies its rules with precision. The title itself contributes to this impression: two words containing ideas of light, heat, exposure, and a mental geography reduced to a few signs. The environmental anxiety identified by the artist adds another layer of tension. Murray allows it to operate beneath the surface of the work. The beauty of the record often arises from this caution, from its ability to suggest a problem through form rather than turning it into a declaration. Islands Alight works as an internal development. Elements that have long been present find a different proportion and produce new consequences. Murray knows his own language well and modifies its rules with precision. ~Mirco Salvadori After repeated listening, the maturity of the project becomes clear: this is the work of a musician deepening his own vocabulary and changing the way it behaves. The rhythmic component opens new possibilities, the attention to detail preserves its coherence, and the emotional dimension finds a more physical balance. Islands Alight seems to define a precise phase in his artistic trajectory. Murray’s poetry emerges from his control of material and his trust in time. A small number of decisions can transform an entire passage. A sound acquires meaning through position, duration, and memory. This precision gives the record an intense yet measured presence. Islands Alight is one of the most accomplished works of James Murray’s recent career. A focused, patient album, capable of expanding his research through rhythm, space, and studio transformation. Murray’s voice remains perfectly recognisable and here finds a new substance. Islands Alight is available on quiet details. The Yasu Ether Project is an overall haunting and pleasant experience, a final document of an artist who understood that darkness and stillness aren’t opposites of beauty but conditions under which a particular kind of beauty becomes possible. César Alexandre knew that instinctively, and this album proves it one last time. A quiet closing chapter The Yasu Ether Project by Mount Shrine   Cryo Chamber has held the bar for exploratory dark ambient music with a cinematic edge since Simon Heath (the artist behind Atrium Carceri) founded the label with a collaborative focus that has become its defining characteristic. The catalog spans deep space drone, horror-influenced soundscapes, Lovecraftian collaborative projects, and the kind of patient, immersive dark ambient that rewards extended, solitary listening. Among its most beloved artists was Mount Shrine—the project of César Alexandre, a Brazilian producer from Rio de Janeiro who grew up absorbing Brian Eno, Burial, Aphex Twin, and Akira Yamaoka‘s score for Silent Hill 2 before finding his own voice in lo-fi field recordings, vinyl crackle, tape hiss, and long meditative drone structures. He debuted on Cryo Chamber with Winter Restlessness in 2018, followed by Ghosts on Broken Pavements in 2019. He also worked under Mount Hibiki and released vaporwave under the name Lindsheaven Virtual Plaza, an early and influential figure in that scene. César Alexandre passed away on April 15, 2021, from COVID-19. He was one of the first artists whose work made people fall in love with ambient music, and the void he left has been felt consistently in the years since. Cryo Chamber has honored his memory carefully—releasing All Roads Lead Home in 2022 and The Mount Hibiki Tapes in 2024, and The Yasu Ether Project arrives now as the final piece of audio he ever sent to Simon Heath. A version had previously appeared on his own Bandcamp before the page closed. Now preserved and released once more, it stands as a quiet closing chapter. There is a somber feeling that comes with reading about this release before you press play, and that feeling doesn’t leave once you do. Listening to this is the last remnant of his feelings and emotions, the final transmission from an artist whose music offered rest, solitude, and quiet escape to everyone who found it. Just like most Cryo Chamber releases you can expect a very dark and soft ride through the entirety of the album, but there is something that peaks through all the darkness, a simple peace that is haunting. You don’t know what it is that’s calming about it. Maybe it’s the field recordings of birds and daytime, the remembrance of what it feels like when you’ve just woken from a bad storm. Unsettling and peaceful at the same time. That’s how it feels listening to this. Unsettling and peaceful at the same time :: “Gaseous Peak” and “Polysunset” are the standouts on this release. The entirety of the album is wrapped in vinyl hiss, that persistent crackle that was always central to Mount Shrine‘s identity, the sound of something being played back from a medium that’s been worn down by time. It gives the record a physical texture, a sense that these recordings exist in a material world even as the music itself drifts away from one. The closing track is something different. The synths here aren’t just simple pads and atmospheric textures like the rest of the album. Little vocal touches, small nothings, barely registered, appear as the pads build. A small key arp plays in and out, and the visual being created in your head as you listen is genuinely peaceful in a way that feels earned after everything that preceded it. The contradiction at the heart of this closing track is what makes it so affecting, the familiar Mount Shrine darkness is still present, but something lighter has been let in, a crack of warmth that sits differently knowing what this release represents. Simon Heath closes the release notes with “May you rest in peace.” There’s nothing to add to that. The Yasu Ether Project is an overall haunting and pleasant experience, a final document of an artist who understood that darkness and stillness aren’t opposites of beauty but conditions under which a particular kind of beauty becomes possible. César Alexandre knew that instinctively, and this album proves it one last time. The Yasu Ether Project is available on Cryo Chamber. items.body: Arca’s latest record pushes her glitch-heavy, genre-defying sound further than ever, turning chaos, vulnerability, and radical experimentation into one of her most fearless works yet. Arca turns chaos into art Throughout her career, Arca has been moving in and out of pop and radical experimentation. If you’ve seen her in concert, you probably know how chaotic it can get, often slipping into the multimedia with a feral mix of live music, DJ-ing, and performance art. A heart-rending a cappella rendition of “Piel” from her 2017 self titled will follow a reggaeton classic, then Aphex Twin’s infamous “Ventolin” will play while she squirts paint on plexiglass and behind her, her face distorts in a thousand ways in glitched up videos. Just in the past year, she’s gone from working on music with mainstay names—producing for none other than Madonna in her return to form Confessions II and remixing for Robyn and Nine Inch Nails—to her first art exhibitions including at the ICA in London, to a new instalment of her NTS project Airdoll. A new album and/or mixtape had been teased for some time now, following a break after the five-part Kick project. Airdoll—aired just two weeks before the release of XXXXX, and a few days before its announcement—showed a glimpse of things to come: a radio mix of largely own music, it included tracks from her previou​s uncategorisable releases @@@@@, ±±±±±, and Disintegrator alongside unreleased music. The flow and selection in Airdoll hinted at a complex, chaotic and experimental direction, in direct contrast to the laser-focused styles of Kick II to V and the accessibility of Puta/Sola. Last year’s double-single, in fact, was widely assumed to be the start of a new album cycle, however XXXXX does not include any previously released material, nor was it preceded by any singles. Rather, it dropped like a bolt out of the ether, or, as album opener “No End” states kicking off the diva experimental FM transmission, it “cut through the horizon with piercing hope”. Swelling strings follow, and pulsing industrial beats, and voices so processed to feel barely human in tracks flowing one into the other with no solution of continuity. It’s clear from the beginning that this album returns to the freeform exploration of earlier Arca releases such as &&&&& and Xen—the intense emotional quality of “Wound” is right there at the onset in “Willow,” with its strings soaring atop a likely sample of the bells from Aphex’s “XMD 5a”—but the truth is that it’s hard to compare XXXXX to anything other than Arca herself, bringing her craft to a logical peak. While some connections to her previous work and to others can be made, such as the aforementioned Aphex, or SOPHIE’s or Autechre’s outrageous sound design (the “Heart”/“Syncope”/“Raver” trifecta a wonderful case in point), or even the nod to Daddy Yankee’s “Rompe” in “Eidolon,” the album is a probing journey into the unknown, led by faith in the human. “Cinch,” the first of a few minute-long narrative respites in XXXXX’s torrential flow, makes this abundantly clear: “And so she wandered beyond the threshold, moving further still into the unknown. Eyes closed. Heart open.” The traveler, merged with a technology of her own making in the Gigerian album cover, has no fear. One of the album’s highlights, the maximalist “Fxck” pushes pop’s catchiness into the extremes of deconstructed club, with a changa tuki propulsor and post-industrial sound design, crude hi-hats bouncing left and right in the stereo field while sub synth surges anchor lyrics on rough sex as a way to kill the Freudian father. “Taconeando” takes the opposite approach, with a bare and dry take on KicK iii’s warped hip hop influence. These two moments at the heart of the album, probably the closest to songs the album has to offer, pave the way to a latter section drifting into emotional and electrifying IDM, with “Grip” offering one of the record’s most passionate and memorable melodies—a piano progression (Arca’s acoustic instrument of choice) on top of dryly cut and harshly flanging synths—and “Everything” almost slipping into flash-core aesthetics with its relentlessness. The album closes on a harrowing and ambiguous note with “Sueño,” a strident number where a raptor voice so distorted it becomes a synth begs to stop, turn away, turn it off. The voice/synth glitches once more into self-reference, duetting with and bleeding into a sample of Arca’s own unreleased demo “Arpia,” or harpy. A frequent proponent of the glitch as philosophy of art and of life, Arca has slit through innumerable systems such as artistic discipline, genre, gender and taste. XXXXX itself glitched from the mixtape format to album status, just like @@@@@ had glitched into the single format, and its tracks happily blip in and out of themselves and their meanings and feelings. The technology bringing on the glitch is that of the Diva: an archetype—half mythological, half psychoanalytical—holding it all together by a golden thread. A Pallas redux, goddess of art, craft and knowledge, warlike and just and now enhanced into the biomechanoid future, riding an impossible spacecraft, escorted by owls. It’s easy to fail to convey her, to not come through with words as a substitute to sound. As Minerva’s owls only spread their wings with the falling of dusk, the glitch is unpredicted, and only fully understandable after the fact. XXXXX is available on XL. items.body: Six tracks, no wasted motion. ARKADA005 doesn’t revive electro; it plugs it back in, turns the voltage up, and lets the machine speak for itself. Drawing on the foundational grammar of electro Marking a welcome return to the furor of contemporary electronic music, London’s Arkada resurfaces with ARKADA005, a six-track workout from Brussels’ Arsonist Recorder and Sigma_ALgebra. This is electro with the futurist chrome stripped back enough to expose the working parts: rolling bass, snapping breaks, brutal low-end pressure and melodies that still know how to carry a tune. The record feels contemporary without straining to prove it, drawing on the foundational grammar of electro while treating that grammar as ​something alive, flexible and available for further damage. Arsonist Recorder takes the first three cuts straight to the machine soul. The rhythms are tight but never sterile, with heavyweight bass movement and synth lines that bring a real sense of propulsion. There is funk here, but it is not nostalgia-funk. It is the physical intelligence of the form: music built to make the body respond while the circuitry does something stranger underneath. Sigma_ALgebra with three tracks that feel like an autopsy performed at club volume. The components are stripped down, isolated and rebuilt into lean, muscular constructions where breaks, bass and synthetic detail lock together with increasingly brutal efficiency. What makes the record work is the tension between its opposing instincts—sweet melody and hard mechanics, precision and abrasion, body-popping unity and 4am chicanery. Six tracks, no wasted motion. ARKADA005 doesn’t revive electro; it plugs it back in, turns the voltage up, and lets the machine speak for itself. Arkada #005 is available on Arkada. items.body: Durable Oxide announces itself with DOX-001—the debut release from a new Portland, Oregon-based label intent on delivering decisive electronic atmospheres. It’s a strong opening statement for a label to make, and Radio Free Money earns it. Textured electronic music with an edge of menace Radio Free Money by Latest Fad   Durable Oxide announces itself with DOX-001—the debut release from a new Portland, Oregon-based label intent on delivering decisive electronic atmospheres. It’s a strong opening statement for a label to make, and Radio Free Money earns it. For a first release, the RIYL speaks volumes: Demdike Stare, Stars of the Lid, The Heartwood Institute, Castles In Space. That’s a specific compass pointing toward slow-burn, cinematic, deeply textured electronic music with an edge of menace, and Latest Fad delivers exactly that. Latest Fad is a duo—Paul Uusitalo and Dan Wilk, members based in Portland, OR and Seattle, WA, who have been collaborating on professional video software together for decades before turning their full attention to music in earnest in 2019. Their previous two albums came out on their own imprint Fading Systems. Radio Free Money is the​ir third full-length and their first on an outside label, employing banks of antiquated synthesizers, modern workstations, analog effects devices, and stringed instruments woven into an electroacoustic pastiche of submerged melodies, hidden rhythms, drops that never arrive, and hopeful/mournful atmospherics. The description “both claustrophobic and infinitely expansive” is apt—this is music that feels like it’s pressing in and opening outward at the same time. Simple ambience, but it works :: At first, Latest Fad is genuinely mysterious—you don’t know what to expect when you press play. This leans toward the ambient experimental side of things but has melodic aspects woven through. “Business Hugs II” arrives as the second track and introduces a static stutter effect that’s immediately intriguing, it opens a conversation the rest of the album keeps having with itself. This plays more as a collective than a conventional album, tracks functioning as interconnected environments rather than separate songs. “Overgrowth Mindset” is one of the most melodic pieces on the release—keys, off-rhythmic tones, and a bassline that brings some light into what is otherwise a consistently dark listening experience. Simple ambience, but it works as contrast against the heavier material surrounding it. “Aberrant Tool & Die” is another interesting piece—its only rhythm is a stable boom with a building single-note cymbal hit, that stale one-note repetition becoming hypnotic as other sounds and effects surface in the background before the track ends in a very dark place. Restraint is the operative word here. The track knows what not to do, and that’s half the work. “Live Laugh Loop” is the favorite of the release—a sad, dark melody with a flanged note sweeping in that makes the intro deliberately hard to parse. The distortion on the pads creates a density that almost obscures the other elements underneath, but those elements are there and they emerge gradually. Nothing here follows a conventional melodic pattern. The only thing obeying musical note rules is the distorted pads themselves—everything surrounding it is off-tone, and that off-tone quality is exactly what gives the track its dark, closing character. As a final statement it lands well. For a label’s debut release, Durable Oxide has set a clear and credible tone. Labels like Castles In Space and The Heartwood Institute built their identities one carefully chosen release at a time, letting the catalog define the aesthetic rather than announcing it upfront. DOX-001 suggests Durable Oxide understands that logic. Radio Free Money is a strong opening argument for what the label intends to be. Radio Free Money is available on Durable Oxide. items.body: From Helsinki’s Toinen kerros comes Isthmus Recordings, a new label and live archive capturing the restless, intimate sounds of Finland’s experimental music scene.   Bringing Helsinki’s Sounds Together Kesän korvalla by Koho / Koskenlahti Ballad Broadcast / Lineaments by Isthmus Recordings   Isthmus Recordings is a new record label based in Helsinki and Venice, also functioning as an archive for performances recorded in Toinen kerros, a new community-driven space for practicing and encountering sonic arts which which (in a few phases), has become a hub for the Finnish experimental music scene. The first two releases by Isthmus (directly funding the space with Bandcamp sales) include performances in genres such as electroacoustic improvisation, ambient, and minimalism. Recorded in May 2025 and fittingly titled Kesän korvalla—“on the verge of summer,” but also “with the ear of summer”—the first Isthmus release is a performance by the duo composed of sound artist J. Koho (whose brilliant designs grace the Isthmus cover arts so far) and percussionist Minna Koskenlahti. During the 35-minute piece, Koho / Koskenlahti improvise with amplified and processed concrète sounds, but also with sounds recalling more standard mallet percussion instruments and, later in the piece, wooden flutes and whistles. The improvised piece is organized in movements, with different moods and textures following one another: first frantic but gentle percussions set the atmosp​here, a drone-oriented phase follows and then vitalistic and almost free-jazz wind instruments loudly pierced the tapestry of drones. After this climax, the piece descends back into percussive territory, increasing in intensity and chaos and then falling back into order with long stretches of metallic sounds finally slowing down into ambiance. There is something meteorological about the piece, coming, growing and going like a weather event—a rush of wind moving natural and human objects before a summer shower, and then going and fading in the distance just as it came. Isthmus documents music in motion :: The second Isthmus release (Ballad Broadcast / Lineaments) so far includes two pieces, respectively a duo performance by Mark Reid Bulatović and Simone Spampinato, and a solo piece in two parts by Fredrik Rasten. The whole release focuses on guitars, and particularly acoustic guitars with uncommon tuning, interacting with ambience rather than effects or found sounds. At the beginning of Bulatović and Spampinato’s piece, “Ballad Broadcast,” the recording lets through room noise—a door opening, people moving, camera shutters—which, while most likely just accidental to the composition, add to the quiet and enigmatic guitar arpeggios. Over twenty minutes, the guitars form a very sparse call and response of sorts between a drier and more plucked sound and a strummed one with softer decay, but while they are in dialogue, they don’t offer an obvious interpretation, and the slice around them takes most of the sonic and semantic space. Fredrik Rasten’s piece, “Lineament” is a performance of the 2023 studio album of the same name. The pieces feature guitar arpeggios as the undisputed protagonists, but also held-note vocals and sine drones adding to the texture and interacting with the guitars’ own resonance and vibrations. While part I chooses simple arpeggios overlapping in their upward and downward trajectories as its main shape, in part two chords also enter the equation, giving a less regular effect and more space to the voice and drone. With forthcoming (and past) events at Toinen kerros including fantastic names both from the Finnish scene and internationally, one should really be looking forward to the live performance series growing—and hopefully more outside of the live archive too. (And if you’re in the Helsinki area, make sure to keep an eye on their programming!) Kesän korvalla and Ballad Broadcast / Lineaments are both available on Isthmus. items.body: Presumed finished after the death of founding member Richard H. Kirk, Cabaret Voltaire have instead returned to the stage with a vengeance, selling out shows, resurrecting old collaborations, and proving that their dark industrial pulse still hits hard in 2026. We caught up with Stephen Mallinder to talk about the reunion, the tour, Richard Kirk, and bringing the Cabs’ music back to life. Cabaret Voltaire rise from ashes But What Time Is It Really? by Cabaret Voltaire CODE (2026 Remastered Digital Deluxe Edition) by Cabaret Voltaire   For a group missing a founding member and presumed kaput for good after his death, Cabaret Voltaire have been busy. But 2026 has been a year of surprises and unexpected reunions. Among them, Cabaret Voltaire shines, with sold-out shows across Europe and the United States. Stephen Mallinder, one of the founding members, hit the stage with Chris Watson, who left the group in the 1980s, for an incredible tour of Europe. Now, Cabaret Voltaire returns to the States as they herald the re-release of CODE, their 1987 industrial dance masterpiece. “It’s been amazing to see the world again on tour,” said Mal as he prepared for their first show in the States on this last leg of their US tour. “The crowds ​are a great mix of people, with fans going way back as well as new fans. It’s been great to see younger folks at the shows really getting into it. Nice to see Cabaret Voltaire continues to bring people out.” Folks who want to hear how the band sounds after all this time can check out But What Time Is It Really?, a live recording from Cabaret Voltaire’s shows in the UK, including Sheffield, where it all began. Mal and company bring the classics to the stage with a new life and vitality. The songs sound very much like live versions fans will know, but with an updated edge that doesn’t rehash the material so much as enliven it, reminding us why their music became popular worldwide and remains so to this day. The themes and lyrics remain harshly relevant and resonant at a time when fascism isn’t being left behind closed doors anymore. “It was a concern when we were coming over to tour the West Coast,” said Mal when asked about visiting the States during a time of authoritarian crackdown. “We didn’t know what to expect. But it’s been okay and nothing out of sorts, really. No hassle playing—nothing like the old days when Mussolini Headkick came out and we had Nazi skinheads showing up to gigs! Those were rough, but we wanted to provoke people, to bring out a reaction, which we certainly did. But we’re not playing out-of-the-way places where people may not know our music. We’ve always played cities like New York, Chicago, or San Francisco, where we have a lot of longtime fans. But in San Francisco, for instance, there was a larger number of trans and gay kids at the show, which was great to see. People coming out to enjoy themselves and express themselves is always good for music and for us. Someone in Poland actually came to a gig dressed as the Microphonies cover, which was a first!”   Louder than ever :: On this leg of the tour, Mal is joined by Benge, a frequent collaborator with Mal among many others; longtime Cabs live member Eric Random; and Tara Busch, who takes over for Chris Watson, who will remain in the UK. “It’s been great playing with Chris again, as well as the rest of the band,” said Mal. “Chris and I are old friends, and we’ve played and toured together a lot. Nowadays it’s more or less the same, except his jokes are more shit than ever (laughs). But seriously, working with Chris and his massive collection of recordings has been incredible. It was interesting for him to learn songs that came after his time, not just ‘Landslide’ and ‘Nag Nag Nag.’ Since there were no stems to work from, Benge and I had to find all the samples with help from Chris.” “Since Chris is sitting out the US tour, Tara Busch has come onboard. Tara is a veteran, so having her come on was a no-brainer, as she’s toured with her band I Speak Machine and has worked with John Foxx and Benge as well,” said Mal. “She works the samples that Chris would, as well as handling other duties. I’ve played with Benge a lot, and Eric has been on The Crackdown and Microphonies as well as on tour with us. It’s a band of old friends.” With such longevity as the Cabs have had, it would be impossible to overlook the absence of Richard H. Kirk, who for several years after Mal’s departure kept use of the band name. As a founding member and one half of the band during their duo era, his absence from the tour is a sad one for fans and the band alike. “No, I don’t think so, sadly,” said Mal when asked if this tour would have been possible when Kirk was alive. “Richard wouldn’t have been interested in doing it with me. Though he did a few shows under the name, it was mostly his own work, from the later albums like Plasticity and International Language. He had an idea that Cabaret Voltaire could be an evolving, changing thing, but then he passed. And one of the things Chris and I wanted to do was not overlook him, but celebrate his part in the music of Cabaret Voltaire. It’s why we start the show with a dedication to him.” Cabaret Voltaire still make noise :: Having rehearsed and then toured the songs for almost a year, are there any plans to release material as the new Cabaret Voltaire? Mal isn’t circumspect. “It’s not like a novelty act or some rehashing of the old hits. In reworking the songs for the tour, we’ve made them so we can play them and have them recognizable, but they’re also new in a way, too. We’ve been recording the shows and lots of video from them as well. We will definitely be releasing some live stuff from it and other things.” The US dates coincide with Mute’s release of CODE, Cabaret Voltaire’s 1987 masterpiece and what some people consider the greatest work of their major-label dance days. “Mute did a fantastic job,” said Mal. “There’s so much material from then that we had to go through, with all the various mixes and remixes and demos from back then. CODE was probably our most overtly political record, which is interesting, touring and playing it in these very different but scary political times.”​ 2026 Final tour dates ::Sept 11 – Dallas, TX – Granada Theater^Sept 12 – Austin, TX – LevitationSept 15 – Chicago, IL –  Metro^Sept 16 – Chicago, IL –  Metro^Sept 18 – Toronto, ON –  Phoenix Concert Theatre^Sept 19 – Montreal, QC – Sat^Sept 21 – Boston, MA – The Wilbur^Sept 25 – New York, NY – Knockdown Center^Sept 26 – Philadelphia, PA –  Underground Arts^Oct 7 – Dublin, The AcademyOct 8 – Belfast, LimelightOct 10 – Birmingham, Town Hall*Oct 11 – Liverpool, Arts Club*Oct 13 – Nottingham, Rock City>Oct 14 – Cardiff, The Globe>Oct 15 – Bath, Forum*Oct 17 – Newcastle, Boiler Shop*Oct 18 – Glasgow, Barrowland*Oct 19 – Manchester, Albert Hall*Oct 21 – Bexhill, De La Warr Pavilion*Oct 22  – London, Roundhouse*Oct 25 – Sheffield, Octagon*^ w/ I Speak Machine*w/ Gazelle Twin> w/ Fader But What Time Is It Really? and CODE (2026 Remastered Digital Deluxe Edition) are both available on Mute. After that is Schooldays, still setting the scene, but in a remarkably Gentle Giant way, including the classic mallet percussion solo. Working all day kicks off the main section of the album and rounds off the A side, and while a little cringey at times, it's easy to put up with for that fantastic keyboard solo in the middle. The B side, however is one of my favorite sides of music of all time, up there with the B side of Foxtrot, In the Land of Grey and Pink, and Fragile. Peel the Paint is undoubtably one of my favorite songs ever, with its rough Derek Shulman vocals and intricate guitar/drums interplay. Then, finishing off the album, Mr. Class and Quality / Three Friends (essentially being one track) is brilliant as well. Derek's vocals are absolute ear candy to me, and I often find myself singing "middleman sees straight ahead and never crosses borders" in random situations. As well as this, I could go on for pages on the masterful narrative, but I can't summarize my opinion into a short enough section. All in all, this is one of my favorite albums to listen to all the way through, and I'm very glad to share my opinion. items.body: Review by martindavey87 — Over 40 years into their careers, and it's pretty likely that no band has ever taken more risks than Metallica. From the initial young phase of "proving yourself", to becoming stadium rock stars, alternative rockers, eyeliner, orchestras, covers albums, a de-tuned nu metal trash can phase, movies, concert movies, collaborations, and having to again prove they can still play metal? one thing has become apparent with Metallica, they always seem most inspired when they're trying new things. News dropped on '72 Seasons' at the end of 2022, completely out of nowhere, when the band announced it and debuted a new music video. That video, 'Lux �terna', sounded great. It was short and to the point. The 1983 thrash vibe was there, James' vocals sounded fantastic, and the writing was polished. If the new album is like this, then count me in! Sadly, it seems 'Lux �terna' was a one-off, because all the other songs follow the same routine of Metallica's last few albums, being massively bloated and overly long. The band pushes the physical CD format to its limit, as usual, with a staggering 77 minute duration of the same repetitive riff, over and over again. Every song repeats the same section for way too long, and it wears thin very fast. It worked great for Metallica in 1988, but since then, progressive metal has evolved and developed, and as much as I love these guys, the longer songs just don't seem to favour them anymore. It's not terrible though, don't get me wrong, there's a few highlights here and there. 'Lux �terna' is genuinely fantastic, and the title track does start off strong, but man, everything just feels so uninspired the longer the album goes on. The same riffs as before, the same lyrics (always involving words rhyming with cyanide), and guitarist Kirk Hammett sounds bored, almost as if each of his solos are forced and lazy. 2008's 'Death Magnetic' was absolutely fantastic, and they just managed to finish milking that sound with 2016's 'Hardwired? to Self Destruct', but it feels like with '72 Seasons', they're back to releasing just "another Metallica album".Don't get me wrong, I love this band, I even think 'St. Anger' was a great album (see, they were inspired then and had something to prove), and I get that Metallica are at a point in their careers where they don't need to prove anything to anyone and can do whatever they want. Sadly, I just don't get much enjoyment from this album. Uninspired and way, way too long. Oh well, I'll still be here supporting them regardless, I just hope whenever they do another album that there'll be more on it that I can enjoy.

The opening track, "I Vow to Thee, My Screen," unfolds with an epic feel reminiscent of Rush, yet it also features symphonic touches and guitar-keyboard counterpoint characteristic of the most refined era of Genesis, featuring Steve Hackett and Tony Banks."Lullaby for Modern Kids, Part 1" creates a highly original acoustic atmosphere, aided by the percussion of the group's fifth member, Alessandro G. Elide. However, the organ and a choir lend an uncanny quality to the mood, as if stepping into a world imagined by Lewis Carroll, while a classical organ solo unfolds alongside a guitar part reminiscent of Pink Floyd. Masterfully employing psychedelic elements, the album addresses various types of addiction, to medication and new technologies, and how all of this distances us from reality; hence its detached, otherworldly quality, as if setting alienation itself to music. Perhaps we stop talking about it precisely when we are already deep within its grip."Lullaby for Modern Kids, Part 2" features delightful acoustic guitar work, and the echoes of early-era Gabriel return with striking force. The album offers a wealth of nuances and tonal colors, reflecting a range of modos, such as "High-Tech Parent," which evokes a Latin-tinged track by the Doobie Brothers. Fierce guitar work, accompanied by organ and percussion, creates moments of hypnotic rhythm, a soundscape the Norwegian quintet explores across both acoustic and electric dimensions.On "Madness and Magic," the interplay between Mellotron and synthesizers builds layers that pave the way for the album's centerpiece, "Heaven in Your Eye."Here, driven once again by synthesizers and Moog, the acoustic opening gives way to an ascent through inner and outer forests, a journey mirrored in the music and the highly expressive vocals. Dark, Black Sabbath-esque hard rock sections provide a stark contrast to Eastern-influenced melodies, where powerful riffs take command. The promise is ultimately fulfilled with sections of high dramatic tension, featuring distorted accelerations and organ followed by guitar, backed by Mellotron, like clouds accompanying lightning during a storm.

items.body: Tundra When I first encountered the wonderful world of AACM, it never occurred to me that any of the composers would be even interested in a bourgeois form as opera. I had, like many listeners, associated the AACM with jazz and improvised musics. Well, I was wrong. AACM was formed to insert African and Black American musics and ideas into the established western classical canon, not to avoid, supplant, or necessarily alter western classical music per se, except to include non-western musical ideas and create new works not dependent on the dominant influence of European cultural hegemony. I had been aware of Anthony Braxton’s forays into theater works and, of course, Anthony Davis is finally getting recognition for his striking operas. But George Lewis, with roots in jazz, extended improvisational techniques, and truly experimental composition here shows us a gentle, entertaining theatrical style that is a heartfelt celebration of the AACM. Afterword is in a way a musical sequel to George Lewis’ essential history of the AACM, “A Power Stronger Than Itself”. Here is a musical retelling of the history of the AACM. It is oral history in song. This fine recording of a live performance is an ideal documentation of this opera. Of course one hopes for more live performance but it is a joy to have this recording stand as definitive, daring the challenge to mount another production, to tell this story again. This is a chamber opera, meaning that it does not require a Wagnerian large romantic orchestra with epic staging and many singers with a huge chorus to boot. Only eight musicians and one conductor, three singers, and a cast of cameos comprise this little very listenable gem.

items.body: Karen LeFrak As an avid listener, I try to be open to new music. As with any journey, guides can be most useful. One of my occasional musical guides is the fabulous guitarist Sharon Isbin. In addition to founding Julliard’s first doctoral program in guitar, and possessing an encyclopedic knowledge of classical guitar literature, Isbin has a keen sense, perhaps even a calling to find and promote substantial new music. So it is with this lovely album of works commissioned by Isbin. Her many commissions and collaborations have ranged from contemporary classical composers to collaborative efforts with artists outside the western classical music mold. In brief, she is not merely a patron/patroness of music but also an actively engaged participant in the process of music making, learning as much as she teaches, identifying with, and supporting her fellow musicians. I had the pleasure of interviewing Ms. Isbin at the time of the release of her Cedille album. Now, I may be inferring too much from that brief interview, but what stays with me is a sense from her of almost parental warmth, insight, and wisdom. So it is with this unabashedly friendly, pretty, and very listenable album. It is apparently the latest in a discography now numbering some 20 plus albums by Ms. LeFrak. Isbin’s radar has guided me to this interesting renaissance woman whose labors include raising prize poodles, writing best selling children’s books, and, more recently, a composer of substantial new music in the western classical mold. Karen LeFrak. This is my first experience of hearing her musical work (having failed to avail myself of a prize poodle or reading one of those children’s books). This album gets its eminently listenable charm from a winning combination of a truly inventive composer (nice orchestration as well) with Isbin’s definitive interpretation drawn from her ability to deeply understand music of any genre. My initial impression (meaning the first minute or so), was of a warmly tonal, ethnically inflected composition. I followed my guide (Isbin) confident that she would not lead me where I did not want to be. Of course, she did not fail me, and shall remain one of my trusted guides. Sharon Isbin There are 5 tracks on this disc. All tracks feature Sharon Isbin as well as the Orchestra of St. Luke’s, ably led by Enrico Lopez-Yañez. The Miami Concerto was a commission for Ms. Isbin as are the two dance inspired works that comprise the last two tracks. They are chamber works with guitar very much similar in inspiration to the concerto. Miami Concerto for Guitar & Chamber Orchestra (World Premiere Recording)1. Bailamos [4:58]2. Romántico [8:16]3. Festivo [4:36] 4. Habanera Nights [3:31] (World Premiere Recording) Sharon Isbin, guitar; Rolando Morales-Matos, guiro; Mariana Ramirez-Alvarado, claves, Javier Diaz, bongos, Peggy Kampmeier, piano; Carter Brey, cello; Victor Pablo Garcia-Gaetán, shaker 5. Urban Tango [4:10] (World Premiere Recording) Sharon Isbin, guitar; Javier Diaz, bongos; Rolando Morales-Matos, guiro; Peggy Kampmeier, piano The first three tracks contain the “Miami Concerto” and the last two tracks are dance movements titled “Habanera Nights” and “Urban Tango”. All are written with Sharon Isbin in mind in 2003-4 and all were premiered in 2024. This recording followed shortly thereafter. The Miami Concerto is a solid addition to the repertoire. It is cast in three movements and feature melodies and rhythms from the musical roots of the Latin and West African World and features a lovely battery of Latin/African instruments supporting the orchestra. The three movements follow the traditional concerto format, fast with a slow introduction, slow, and fast. The style is well described by the album’s title, “Romantico”. The Habanera and Tango are chamber works featuring Isbin’s guitar. Both, like the concerto derive from the composer’s interest in these melodies and rhythms that have become a part of Miami culture. I’ve listened to this release many times and played it for some friends and colleagues. The consensus, which resonates with my personal opinion, is that this is a great recording.
